runs.question: prism-figure_layout
runs.text:
Figure 3 illustrates the complete pipeline of **Prism** (Precision-aware Reweighting and Internalization for Skilled Manipulation) [¶54]. The overall framework tackles *Flow-Time Starvation*—the tendency of standard flow matching to under-supervise brief, submillimeter manipulation stages—by extracting precision demands from demonstration trajectories and using them to reallocate action loss supervision and shape VLM features [¶10][¶54]. Crucially, all precision-forcing components operate strictly during training, leaving the policy backbone and inference ODE integration unchanged [¶54][¶57].

[[part 1]]

### (a) Proprioceptive Precision Scoring (PPS)
The left panel details the offline extraction of the precision score \(\rho_i \in [0,1]\) prior to training [¶57][¶59]. PPS does not require privileged simulator data or tactile sensors; instead, it derives precision demand from standard demonstration trajectories [¶59][¶146]. It monitors joint motion \(\Delta q_i\) and end-effector displacement \(\Delta e_i\) to compute relative slowness within an episode [¶60][¶61]. It then gates this with gripper engagement \(g_i^{\mathrm{eng}}\) and motion validity factors \(t_i\) (which filter out rapid gripper closing or pauses) [¶61][¶62]. The resulting color strip at the bottom shows that coarse transport stages (like cable pickup) receive low scores (blue/green), while fine alignment and insertion stages receive peak precision scores (orange/red) [¶54][¶62].

[[part 2]]

### Base Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Backbone
The top-right region depicts the underlying policy architecture [¶54]. Multimodal inputs—including multi-view camera frames through a Vision Encoder, natural-language instructions, and discretized proprioceptive state tokens—are processed by a pretrained Vision Language Model (VLM) [¶18][¶54]. The VLM produces prefix hidden states that condition an iterative Action Expert (e.g., a diffusion or flow-matching transformer) [¶18][¶54]. During generation, the Action Expert denoises a noisy action chunk along flow time \(\tau\) into an executable action chunk [¶18][¶30][¶54].

[[part 3]]

### Conditional Precision Regularization (CPR)
The lower-middle panel shows how Prism internalizes precision awareness into the VLM condition representation [¶54][¶71]. The VLM prefix hidden states are processed with a mask-aware mean pooling layer to produce a pooled condition feature \(h_{c_i}\) [¶54][¶71]. A lightweight auxiliary MLP head (Linear \(\to\) SiLU \(\to\) Linear \(\to\) Sigmoid) predicts the scalar precision demand \(\hat{\rho}(c_i)\) [¶72][¶156]. By minimizing the mean squared error \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR}} = (\hat{\rho}(c_i) - \rho_i)^2\), gradients update the VLM backbone so its latent representations learn to recognize when physical precision is required [¶71][¶72]. This auxiliary predictor is discarded after training [¶57].

[[part 4]]

### Precision-Scaled Weighting (PSW) & Combined Loss
The lower-right panel shows how action supervision is concentrated where it matters most [¶54][¶65]. Standard flow-matching loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}\) uniformly penalizes velocity errors [¶31][¶68]. PSW computes a sample weight \(w_i = 1 + \gamma \rho_i \Psi_i\) [¶66], combining:
1. **Offline Precision Demand \(\rho_i\)** from PPS [¶65][¶66].
2. **Flow-time Visibility \(\Psi_i\)**, defined as \((1 - \tau_i)^p (1 - e^{-\mathrm{SNR}_i / \tau_0})\) [¶66]. This combines clean-end emphasis (since errors near \(\tau=0\) have the largest physical endpoint impact) with an action RMS-based SNR gate that prevents amplifying noise before actual action signals emerge [¶46][¶49][¶65][¶69].

The reweighted flow-matching loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PSW}}\) and the regularization loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR}}\) form the total training objective \(\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PSW}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{CPR}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR}}\) [¶74]. Because the predicted \(\hat{\rho}\) does not feed back into sample weighting \(w_i\), training remains stable and decoupled [¶57][¶73].

runs.text:
The paper reports neither figure — no dollar cost and no CO₂ tonnage appear anywhere in it. What it does give, in Section 6.3, is an energy estimate that you would need as a starting point for either number:

**What the paper states**
- The logged production training segments total roughly **2 million GPU-hours**, or about **1.1 GWh**, broken down as ~225,000 GPU-hours for the 8B continued-pretraining stages, ~1.5 million for the 70B stages, and the remainder for the long-context extensions of both models [¶370]. The per-phase GPU-hour counts come from Table 40 [¶368].
- For scale, this compares with roughly 5 GWh for the from-scratch Apertus 1.0 pretraining, and over the whole project duration 9 million GPU-hours were allocated, an estimated 5 GWh [¶370].
- These estimates cover only the logged production segments: they exclude post-training, evaluation, ablations, and idle reservation time [¶370].

**On the carbon footprint specifically**
The paper never converts energy to tonnes of CO₂. It notes only that Alps draws on carbon-free hydropower and is cooled with lake water in a closed cycle [¶370]. So while the operational electricity-related emissions are presumably near zero for Scope 2, the paper does not quantify any CO₂ figure — neither operational nor embodied — and I can't infer one from what it states.

**On dollar cost**
The paper contains no monetary figures for the training campaign at all. Any dollar estimate would require assumptions the paper doesn't supply (e.g., a rental price per GH200 GPU-hour, the actual fraction of the 9 million allocated GPU-hours used, staffing, storage, etc.), so I'd be speculating outside the paper if I attached a number. If you want a rough external estimate, ~2M GH200 GPU-hours at typical cloud GPU-hour prices would give an order of magnitude, but that is clearly not something the paper itself claims.

runs.question: dpo-detail
runs.text:
For the Reddit TL;DR summarization run they used **β = 0.5**, the **RMSprop** optimizer with a **learning rate of 1e-6**, and a **batch size of 64** (Appendix B, [¶201]).

Details from the paper:

- **β (KL-temperature):** β = 0.5 specifically for TL;DR summarization; β = 0.1 is the default for all other settings ([¶201]). Elsewhere the paper notes they did not meaningfully tune β for summarization, so results may underestimate DPO's potential (Section 6.2, [¶67]).
- **Optimizer:** RMSprop ([¶201]).
- **Learning rate:** 1e-6, with a linear warmup from 0 to 1e-6 over the first 150 steps ([¶201]).
- **Batch size:** 64 ([¶201]).
- **Reference policy:** The base model is a GPT-J SFT model fine-tuned on human-written forum post summaries (Section 6, [¶58]; Section 6.2, [¶67]), which they take as π_ref = π_SFT since the preference data was sampled from an SFT model ([¶38]).

All other hyperparameters for the summarization run match the defaults listed in Appendix B ([¶201]). Note that the learning-rate warmup (150 steps) is stated in [¶201] as applying generally, so it should apply to the summarization run too, since "the rest of the parameters remain the same."

runs.question: dpo-figure
runs.text:
No — the plot does not show DPO as the only curve above the 50% line. Best of 128 sits above the dashed 0.5-parity line at **every** temperature shown, and at the lowest temperature (0.25) DPO itself is still *below* 0.5 and roughly 15 points below Best of 128. DPO only catches up at temperatures 0.75 and 1.0, where the two methods are within each other's error bars (DPO nominally ahead at 1.0). The caption's claim is accurate only for the *fine-tuned* policies — which is how the body text states it: "DPO is the only computationally efficient method that improves over the preferred completions in the Anthropic-HH dataset" [¶68].

[[part 1]]

The left panel plots GPT-4 win rate against the dataset's chosen (human-preferred) responses, so the dashed line at 0.5 marks parity with those chosen completions [¶59][¶68]. Reading the three evaluated temperatures (values approximate, read off the plot):

- **Temp 0.25:** Best of 128 ≈ 0.54, already above parity; DPO ≈ 0.38, below the line. DPO is clearly worse here.
- **Temp 0.75:** both ≈ 0.60 — a tie within error bars.
- **Temp 1.0:** DPO ≈ 0.62–0.63 vs Best of 128 ≈ 0.61 — DPO nominally ahead, but error bars overlap.

Two other things are visible: Best of 128 is nearly flat across temperature while DPO climbs monotonically over the plotted range; and Preferred-FT peaks around 0.43 (never reaching parity) while the 2-shot prompted Pythia-2.8B base model sits at 0.16–0.25. So among *trained* methods DPO is indeed the only one above the line — but Best of 128 is above it too. (The PPO-trained RLHF model doesn't appear at all because the authors couldn't find any prompt or temperature where it beat the base Pythia-2.8B [¶68].)

[[part 2]]

The right panel shows DPO's win rate at sampling temperatures 1.0 and 0.7 over ~3300 fine-tuning steps. Both curves start well below 0.5 (≈0.33–0.38), cross parity by roughly step 300, and then fluctuate between ≈0.55 and ≈0.64 with no clear upward or downward trend, tracking each other closely. This is the evidence for the caption's "fairly stable over the course of training" claim and the paper's remark that DPO converges to near-best performance quickly [¶68]; the mid-training dips are what the discussion flags as a possible instance of reward over-optimization, left as an open question [¶78].

**Reconciling caption and plot**

- Read literally, the caption [¶60] is wrong: Best of 128 clears 0.5 at all three temperatures, so DPO is not the only method above the line — and DPO itself is below the line at temperature 0.25.
- The body text gives the intended, qualified claim: DPO is the only **computationally efficient** method that beats the preferred completions, and it "provides similar or better performance to the computationally demanding Best of 128 baseline" [¶68]. Best of 128 is not a fine-tuned policy — it samples 128 completions per prompt at test time and returns the one a learned reward model scores highest, which the paper calls computationally impractical [¶62], and it serves as a rough proxy for PPO-level performance [¶68].
- Note also that "similar or better" is exactly what the plot shows: DPO is *worse* than Best of 128 at 0.25, comparable at 0.75, and slightly ahead at 1.0. (Minor caption slip: it says "chosen summaries", but this panel is dialogue — the baseline is the chosen response [¶59].)

parts.label: Left: win rate vs temperature
parts.note: GPT-4 win rate against the chosen Anthropic-HH responses at sampling temperatures 0.25, 0.75 and 1.0. The dashed 0.5 line is parity with the chosen completions; Best of 128 is above it at every temperature, DPO crosses it only at 0.75 and above, while Preferred-FT and Pythia-2.8B never reach it.

parts.label: Right: win rate over training
parts.note: DPO's win rate at sampling temperatures 1.0 and 0.7 over about 3300 fine-tuning steps. Both curves rise past 0.5 within a few hundred steps and then fluctuate between roughly 0.55 and 0.64 with no strong trend.

runs.question: dpo-visual
runs.text:
Here's the whole step: DPO needs only one forward pass through two models per pair, then a plain classification loss — no sampling, no RL loop [¶38]. The loss is defined per pair \((x, y_w, y_l)\), so one training example is exactly one preference pair from the offline dataset \(\mathcal{D}\) [¶18][¶33].

## The step, in words

1. **Take one pair from the data.** A prompt \(x\), a preferred completion \(y_w\), a dispreferred one \(y_l\), labelled by humans [¶18].
2. **Score both completions twice.** Run them through the policy \(\pi_\theta\) (the model being trained) and the frozen reference \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) (a copy of the SFT model, when available [¶38]), giving the four log-probabilities.
3. **Turn log-probs into implicit rewards.** For each completion,
   \[ \hat{r}_\theta(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)}, \]
   the reward implicitly defined by the two models [¶38][¶42]. No separate reward network is ever trained.
4. **Compute the loss on the pair** (Eq. 7 [¶33]):
   \[ \mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma\!\left(\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_w) - \hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l)\right) = -\log\sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}\right). \]
   It is just binary cross-entropy on the *margin* between the two implicit rewards.
5. **Backprop and step.** The gradient raises \(\log \pi(y_w \mid x)\), lowers \(\log \pi(y_l \mid x)\), and each pair is scaled by \(\sigma\big(\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l) - \hat{r}_\theta(x, y_w)\big)\) — large exactly when the implicit reward currently ranks the pair wrong [¶37]. Without this weight, a naive ratio objective makes the model degenerate [¶38].

## Details worth noticing

- **Only \(\pi_\theta\) updates.** The reference model's log-probs are constants for the gradient — in the paper's PyTorch code the reference rewards are `.detach()`-ed [¶200].
- **\(\beta\) sets the KL leash.** It scales both the rewards and the effective deviation from \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) [¶24]; the paper defaults to \(\beta = 0.1\) (0.5 for TL;DR summarization), batch size 64, RMSprop at \(1\mathrm{e}{-6}\) [¶201].
- **In practice** many such pairs form a batch; the expectation in Eq. 7 is just the average of these per-pair losses over \(\mathcal{D}\) [¶33].

Now the diagram:

runs.question: mamba-equation
runs.text:
Equation (4) is the **zero-order hold (ZOH) discretization rule** (Section 2, "Discretization" [¶25][¶26]). It is the bridge between the continuous-time SSM and the discrete recurrence the model actually runs:

\[
\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} \;=\; \exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}), \qquad
\overline{\boldsymbol{B}} \;=\; (\Delta \boldsymbol{A})^{-1}\big(\exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}) - \boldsymbol{I}\big)\,\Delta \boldsymbol{B}
\]

**What it computes.** The SSM is defined as a continuous linear system \(h'(t) = \boldsymbol{A}h(t) + \boldsymbol{B}x(t)\) (Eq. 1a [¶24]), but the model must process a sequence one token at a time. Eq. (4) converts the "continuous parameters" \((\Delta, \boldsymbol{A}, \boldsymbol{B})\) into the "discrete parameters" \((\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})\) used in the recurrence \(h_t = \overline{\boldsymbol{A}}h_{t-1} + \overline{\boldsymbol{B}}x_t\) (Eq. 2a [¶24][¶25]). The name "zero-order hold" comes from the assumption that the input \(x(t)\) is held *constant* over each step of length \(\Delta\) — the standard ZOH derivation (not spelled out in the paper) solves the ODE exactly under that assumption:

\[
h(t+\Delta) = \exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})\,h(t) + \int_0^\Delta e^{s\boldsymbol{A}}\,\boldsymbol{B}\,x\,ds,
\qquad \int_0^\Delta e^{s\boldsymbol{A}}ds = \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}(e^{\Delta\boldsymbol{A}} - \boldsymbol{I}),
\]

and rewriting \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1} = \Delta(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})^{-1}\) gives exactly the \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}\) in Eq. (4). So it is the *exact* discrete equivalent for a piecewise-constant input.

**Each symbol:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| \(\boldsymbol{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) | State transition matrix — how the latent state \(h\) evolves on its own. Structured (diagonal in practice) for efficiency [¶33]. |
| \(\boldsymbol{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}\) | Input matrix — how the current input \(x_t\) is written into the state. |
| \(\Delta\) | Step size (timestep). Fixed in prior SSMs; **input-dependent** in Mamba via \(s_\Delta(x)=\mathrm{Broadcast}_D(\mathrm{Linear}_1(x))\), \(\tau_\Delta=\mathrm{softplus}\) [¶56]. |
| \(\exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})\) | Matrix exponential — the exact solution operator of \(h' = \boldsymbol{A}h\) over a duration \(\Delta\); acts as a decay factor on the previous state. |
| \(\boldsymbol{I}\) | The \(N\times N\) identity matrix. |
| \((\Delta\boldsymbol{A})^{-1}\) | Inverse of \(\Delta\boldsymbol{A}\); enters because the input's contribution is integrated over the step. With diagonal \(\boldsymbol{A}\), both \(\exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})\) and this term are computed entrywise. |
| \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}}\) | The discrete transition and input matrices in the recurrence (Eq. 2a). Note \(\boldsymbol{C}\) is not discretized — it reads the state out at each step, \(y_t = \boldsymbol{C}h_t\) [¶24]. |

**Why it matters in Mamba.** The paper's key point is that \(\Delta\) acts as a *generalized RNN gate* through this equation. In the special case \(N=1, \boldsymbol{A}=-1, \boldsymbol{B}=1\) with input-dependent \(\Delta\), the ZOH formulas collapse to a gated update \(h_t = (1-g_t)h_{t-1} + g_t x_t\) with \(g_t = \sigma(\mathrm{Linear}(x_t))\) — Theorem 1, Eq. (5) [¶84][¶85], derived step by step in Appendix C by plugging into Eq. (4) [¶362][¶364]. Intuitively, since eigenvalues \(\lambda\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) map to \(e^{\Delta\lambda}\): a large \(\Delta\) shrinks \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}\) toward 0 (reset the state, focus on the current input) while a small \(\Delta\) keeps \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}\approx 1\) (persist the state, ignore the input) [¶93]. This is why the authors make \(\Delta\) selective but leave \(\boldsymbol{A}\) fixed: \(\boldsymbol{A}\) affects the model only through its interaction with \(\Delta\) in \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = \exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})\) [¶94].

Mechanically, the paper suggests viewing discretization as simply the first step of the forward-pass computation graph [¶27]; it also carries side benefits such as resolution invariance and proper normalization [¶27], and alternative rules or direct parameterization of \((\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})\) are possible [¶25][¶27].

runs.question: prism-figure_layout
runs.text:
Figure 3 (¶54) is the system overview of Prism, and its single connecting thread is the precision score \(\rho\): panel (a) computes it offline from the robot's own demonstration trajectories, and panel (b) spends it in exactly two places during training — as the regression target for CPR (so the VLM representation learns to *recognize* precision demand) and as an input to the PSW weight (so the flow-matching loss is *amplified* where demand is high and action evidence is visible). The backbone in the middle of panel (b) — Vision Language Model plus flow-matching Action Expert — is drawn deliberately untouched: Prism changes only the training objective, and inference runs exactly as in a standard \(\pi_{0.5}\)-style policy [¶57][¶75].

[[part 1]]
Panel (a), top: where the score comes from. The three timestamped frames — cable pickup, bimanual handover, connector insertion — are the stages of the real drive-insertion task whose tolerances Figure 2 analyzed [¶53]. Below them, the "Trajectory-derived signals" box shows the only inputs PPS uses: joint motion and end-effector motion waveforms, combined into "relative slowness", and the gripper-engagement step signal, combined into "motion validity". These map directly to Section 3.2: the displacements \(\Delta q_i\) and \(\Delta e_i\) are mixed into \(s_i\) and rank-converted into \(\mathrm{slow}_i\), while the engagement and gating terms form \(t_i\), giving \(\rho_i = g_i^{\mathrm{eng}}\,\mathrm{slow}_i\,t_i\) [¶60][¶61][¶62]. Both paths converge in the blue PPS block.

[[part 2]]
Panel (a), bottom: the score itself. PPS outputs "Offline Precision Demand \(\rho\)", a continuous per-frame value in \([0,1]\), drawn as color bars under two demonstration strips. Read the bars against the "Low → High" colorbar: the first strip stays mostly cool (routine transport), while the second shows warm orange/red bursts concentrated in the later frames — the precision-critical alignment and insertion segment. This matches the reported behavior that PPS highlights fine-operation intervals in mixed coarse–fine trajectories [¶100]. Crucially, these labels are computed once, before optimization, and then fixed [¶57][¶63]; Appendix B gives the smoothing, gating, and clipping details [¶153][¶154][¶155].

[[part 3]]
Panel (b), top: the backbone Prism does not modify. Camera frames pass through the Vision Encoder into pink tokens; the language instruction ("Insert the cable into the motor drive.") becomes blue tokens; the discretized proprioceptive state ("[STATE] 79 66 212 …") becomes teal tokens; all three token groups enter the Vision Language Model. On the right, a Noisy Action chunk (the wavy series) is concatenated with the VLM output in the Action Expert, which learns the velocity field integrated from \(\tau=1\) (noise) to \(\tau=0\) (clean actions) [¶29][¶30]. This is the standard VLM-plus-flow-matching architecture; Prism adds no inference-time module to it [¶57][¶75].

[[part 4]]
The CPR sub-panel, lower center: teaching the condition to predict demand. The VLM's prefix hidden states (pink squares, one dashed out as padding) come with a 0/1 prefix padding mask (shown as 1, 1, 0, …, 1); mask-aware mean pooling turns them into one pooled condition feature. A lightweight head — Linear → SiLU → Linear → Sigmoid — outputs the predicted demand \(\hat{\rho}\), and the two color bars below show \(\hat{\rho}\) being regressed against the offline \(\rho\) (that squared difference is \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR}}\) [¶71][¶72]). The mask is what makes pooling well-posed for variable-length prefixes. This head works well in practice: on held-out insertion frames it reaches Spearman/Pearson correlations of 0.915/0.931 with MAE 0.056 [¶100].

[[part 5]]
The PSW sub-panel, lower right: reallocating action supervision. Two signals build the gate: the GT action chunk yields its Action RMS (\(\sigma_f\) in the SNR definition [¶47]) and the Flow-time gradient bar gives \(\tau\); together they form "Flow-time Visibility \(\Psi\)", the saturating Poisson-gate probability \(1-e^{-\mathrm{SNR}/\tau_0}\) that delays amplification until the noisy interpolation actually contains usable action evidence [¶49][¶50][¶69]. The offline Precision Demand \(\rho\) enters separately, and "Precision Weighting" fuses everything into \(w_i = 1+\gamma\rho_i\Psi_i\), which multiplies the flow-matching loss \(\mathcal{L}_{FM}\) (the arrow arriving from the output action above) to produce the precision-weighted loss [¶66][¶68]. Since \(w_i\in[1,1+\gamma]\), PSW only ever adds supervision to precision-demanding samples, never withdraws it [¶67].

[[part 6]]
The bottom connector: one combined objective. The dashed arrows from CPR's regression loss and PSW's precision-weighted loss meet at the "Combined Training Objective", \(\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PSW}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{CPR}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR}}\) [¶74]. Note the directionality: PSW always consumes the offline \(\rho\), never CPR's prediction \(\hat{\rho}\), so sample weighting stays independent of what the model currently believes [¶57][¶73]. After training, the predictor head and the \(\rho\) labels are simply discarded, leaving the backbone and its standard ODE solver untouched [¶57]. The whole design adds only four scalars (\(p,\tau_0,\gamma,\lambda_{\mathrm{CPR}}\)) [¶75], and Table 4 ablates the pieces cumulatively on drive insertion: 0.35 → 0.45 (CPR) → 0.70 (+\(\rho\)) → 0.85 (+\(\tau\)) → 0.95 (+SNR) [¶95].

parts.label: PPS inputs
parts.note: Three drive-insertion stages run along a time axis, feeding the trajectory-derived signals box: joint and end-effector motion combine into relative slowness, gripper engagement into motion validity. Both paths enter the Proprioceptive Precision Scoring (PPS) block.

parts.label: Offline precision demand
parts.note: PPS outputs a per-frame demand score rho drawn as color bars under two demonstration strips; warm bursts mark the precision-critical insertion frames. The Low-to-High colorbar at the bottom decodes the scale.

parts.label: VLA backbone
parts.note: The unchanged backbone: images pass through the Vision Encoder, language and discretized state tokens join them in the Vision Language Model, and a noisy action chunk enters the Action Expert that integrates the velocity field to the clean chunk.

parts.label: CPR branch
parts.note: Conditional Precision Regularization: prefix hidden states and their 0/1 padding mask go through mask-aware mean pooling; a small Linear-SiLU-Linear-Sigmoid head predicts demand rho-hat, regressed against the offline rho below.

parts.label: PSW branch
parts.note: Precision-Scaled Weighting: the GT action chunk yields Action RMS and the flow-time bar gives tau; together they build the Flow-time Visibility gate Psi, which combines with demand rho into the weight multiplying the flow-matching loss L_FM.

parts.label: Combined objective
parts.note: The dashed arrows from the CPR regression loss and the PSW precision-weighted loss meet at the Combined Training Objective, summing the weighted flow-matching loss and the CPR term; nothing here changes inference.

runs.question: apertus-synthesis
runs.text:
**No.** The released 8B scores 50.5 on RULER at 262,144 tokens, about 4.3 points below the 54.8 it had before SFT.

**How big the drop was:** After the 16,384-token SFT, the RULER score at 262,144 tokens fell from 54.8 to 8.3, a loss of about 46.5 points (roughly 85%) [¶191]. The paper says short-context scores were unaffected [¶191], but Table 36 shows smaller declines at 8k (85.9 to 83.1) and 16k (81.3 to 77.6) [¶330]. That is worth keeping in mind when reading the "unaffected" claim.

**The fix:** The authors ran a dedicated long-context SFT stage at the full 262,144-token length, following a staged recipe from Qwen 2.5 and Nemotron 3 Nano Omni [¶191]. It kept the production SFT learning rate, held constant at 6×10⁻⁵ for the 8B, with 195 warmup steps and a global batch size of 32 sequences [¶191]. The data is described in Section 4.3 and Table 8 [¶193]. After this stage they evaluated checkpoints across lengths and picked the best one to carry into RL [¶191].

**Recovery through post-training (Table 36, 8B, RULER at 256k):** [¶330]

| Stage | RULER 256k |
|---|---|
| Pre-SFT (long-context pretrained base) | 54.8 |
| After SFT | 8.3 |
| After long-context SFT | 44.9 |
| After RL | 48.8 |
| After DPO | 50.4 |
| After SDPO (released 8B) | 50.5 |

Long-context SFT recovers most of the loss, and RL and preference optimization add a few more points. The paper notes that RL and DPO improve RULER even though neither trains on long documents [¶329]. The released 8B includes the SDPO stage [¶231], so its final score is 50.5.

The paper reports neither a dollar cost nor a carbon footprint in tonnes of CO2. It gives only energy figures, and it says the cluster runs on carbon-free power.

- **Energy (logged segments):** About 1.1 GWh for the continued-pretraining and long-context runs of both models, roughly 2 million GPU-hours. This covers only the logged production segments and excludes post-training, evaluation, ablations, and idle reservation time [¶370].
- **Energy (whole project):** The paper says 9 million GPU-hours were allocated across the project, which it converts to about 5 GWh. This is the closest the paper comes to a total, but it still excludes idle time and other projects' resources [¶370].
- **Method:** Energy is estimated as measured GPU-hours times an assumed 560 W per GH200 module, below the 660 W cap [¶370].
- **Carbon:** The paper says Alps draws on carbon-free hydropower and cools with lake water [¶370]. That implies low operational emissions, but it gives no emission factor or tonnes figure. Converting energy to CO2 would require a carbon intensity that the paper does not provide.
- **Cost:** No monetary cost appears anywhere in the paper. The GPU-hour and energy figures above are the only resource numbers it gives.

runs.question: dpo-derivation
runs.text:
The paper's shortcut is the chain rule plus the sigmoid identity \(\sigma'(u)=\sigma(u)(1-\sigma(u))\). The sigma weight comes out as \(\sigma(-u)\), which equals \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\), the form written in Section 4 [¶37]. Appendix A.4 gives the same steps [¶169–¶173], but its sign conventions are inconsistent with Eq. 7, as noted below.

**Setup**

Let \(\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\) [¶38], and define the margin

\[ u = \hat r_\theta(x,y_w)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) = \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}. \]

Per example, Eq. 7 is \(\ell = -\log\sigma(u)\) [¶33].

**Steps**

1. **Chain rule on the loss.** Differentiating \(-\log\sigma(u)\) gives
\[ \nabla_\theta \ell = -\frac{\sigma'(u)}{\sigma(u)}\,\nabla_\theta u. \]
This is the form the appendix uses in Eq. 22 [¶171–¶172].

2. **Sigmoid identity.** Substituting \(\sigma'(u)=\sigma(u)(1-\sigma(u))\) cancels the \(\sigma(u)\) in the denominator:
\[ \nabla_\theta \ell = -(1-\sigma(u))\,\nabla_\theta u = -\sigma(-u)\,\nabla_\theta u, \]
using \(1-\sigma(u)=\sigma(-u)\) [¶172].

3. **Gradient of the margin.** The reference log-probabilities do not depend on \(\theta\), so only the policy terms survive:
\[ \nabla_\theta u = \beta\big(\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)-\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)\big). \]

4. **Combine and average.** Substituting step 3 into step 2 and taking the expectation over \(\mathcal D\):
\[ \nabla_\theta\mathcal L_{\text{DPO}} = -\beta\,\mathbb E_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\sigma\big(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\big)\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)-\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)\big]\Big]. \]
Since \(\sigma(-u)=\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\), this is the Section 4 expression [¶37].

**Interpretation**

The weight \(\sigma(-u)\) is near 1 when the implicit reward ranks the dispreferred answer higher, and near 0 when it already ranks the preferred answer clearly higher. This is the "higher weight when reward estimate is wrong" annotation in [¶37].

**Sign inconsistency in the appendix**

Eq. 21 [¶169] and the final line of A.4 [¶173] write the sigmoid argument with the roles of \(y_w\) and \(y_l\) swapped relative to Eq. 7. Following that version literally produces a weight \(\sigma(u)\), not \(\sigma(-u)\). Starting from Eq. 7 as written, the correct weight is \(\sigma(-u)\), so the Section 4 form is the right one. The main text's Eq. 7 [¶33] and Section 4 [¶37] agree with each other; the appendix's sign is the outlier.

runs.question: dpo-detail
runs.text:
For the TL;DR summarization DPO run, use **β = 0.5**, **RMSprop**, **learning rate 1e-6**, and **batch size 64**. Appendix B gives these settings.

- **Beta:** The default is β = 0.1, but "For TL;DR summarization, we use β = 0.5, while rest of the parameters remain the same" [¶201].
- **Optimizer and learning rate:** RMSprop with learning rate 1e-6, linearly warmed up from 0 over the first 150 steps [¶201].
- **Batch size:** 64 [¶201].
- **Reference model:** Set π_ref to the SFT model. The authors say that because the preference data was sampled from π^SFT, they initialize π_ref = π^SFT when it is available [¶38]. For summarization they use a public SFT checkpoint (CarperAI's openai_summarize_tldr_sft, footnote 2) [¶58, ¶272].

The paper also says β was not meaningfully tuned for summarization, so the authors suspect DPO's results may underestimate its potential [¶67]. Section 6.1 swept β ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 1, 5} only for the controlled sentiment task [¶64].

The paper does not state the number of training steps or epochs, the hardware, or whether the loss is averaged or summed over the batch, so you would need to choose those yourself or check the released code.

runs.question: dpo-figure
runs.text:
**No.** The left plot does not show DPO as the only method above 50%. Best of 128 is above 0.5 at every temperature, and DPO is above it only at the higher temperatures. The caption's wording overstates the result. The text is more careful: DPO is "the only *computationally efficient* method" that improves over the preferred completions [¶68].

**DPO vs. Best of 128 at each temperature** (values read by eye from the plot, so approximate; the three temperature points are about 0.25, 0.7 and 1.0 [F1, ¶60]):

- **Temperature 0.25:** Best of 128 is about 0.54 and DPO about 0.37. Best of 128 is clearly higher, and only Best of 128 is above the 0.5 line.
- **Temperature ~0.7:** DPO is about 0.60 and Best of 128 about 0.60. They are effectively tied.
- **Temperature 1.0:** DPO is about 0.63 and Best of 128 about 0.61. DPO is slightly higher, but the error bars overlap.

So DPO's curve crosses Best of 128 between the lowest temperature and about 0.7, and at the higher temperatures DPO is at or slightly above it. The gap there is small relative to the error bars, so the plot does not establish that DPO is better.

**Other methods:** Preferred-FT (about 0.30, 0.42, 0.37) and Pythia-2.8B (about 0.16, 0.25, 0.21) stay below 0.5 at every temperature.

**Why the caption differs from the plot:** Best of 128 is a much more expensive baseline. It samples 128 completions per query and picks the best under a learned reward [¶62, ¶68]. The paper's claim is that DPO matches or beats it at a fraction of the cost, not that DPO beats every method. The caption also calls the comparison "chosen summaries," though this is a dialogue experiment; the plot's own title refers to the chosen completions [¶60, ¶68].

runs.question: dpo-visual
runs.text:
The DPO step turns one labeled pair into a single loss: the policy is pushed to raise the implicit reward of the preferred completion relative to the rejected one, with no reward model and no sampling during training.

**The pipeline for one pair**

1. **Data.** Each training example is a prompt \(x\), a preferred completion \(y_w\), and a dispreferred completion \(y_l\), taken from an offline dataset \(\mathcal{D}\) ([¶38]; [¶20]).
2. **Two models score both completions.** The trainable policy \(\pi_\theta\) and a frozen reference \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) (usually the SFT model) each give log-probabilities for \(y_w\) and \(y_l\) given \(x\) ([¶38]; Appendix B code, [¶200]).
3. **Log-ratios.** For each completion, take \(\log \pi_\theta(y \mid x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\).
4. **Implicit reward.** Scale each log-ratio by \(\beta\). This gives \(\hat r_\theta(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)}\), the reward implicitly defined by the language model ([¶38]).
5. **Margin and loss.** The per-pair loss is the negative log-sigmoid of the reward gap, as in Eq. (7) ([¶33]):

\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\!\left(\hat r_\theta(x,y_w) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_l)\right)
\]

6. **Update.** Backpropagate through \(\pi_\theta\) only and take an optimizer step. Appendix B reports \(\beta = 0.1\), batch size 64, and RMSprop at learning rate \(10^{-6}\) with warmup ([¶201]).

**What the gradient does**

The gradient raises the likelihood of \(y_w\) and lowers the likelihood of \(y_l\). Each pair is weighted by \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\), so pairs the implicit reward already orders correctly contribute little, and pairs it gets wrong contribute more ([¶37]; derivation in Appendix A.4 [¶173]).

**Why it is simpler than RLHF**

RLHF first fits a reward model and then runs RL against it. DPO replaces that with a change of variables, so the same Bradley-Terry objective becomes a classification-style loss on the policy ([¶10]; [¶30]–[¶33]). The paper's Section 6 results come from the Section 6 experiments, not from this single-pair walkthrough. I have not checked any results beyond what the paper reports.

runs.question: mamba-equation
runs.text:
Equation (4) is the **zero-order hold (ZOH)** rule. It converts the continuous-time SSM parameters \((\Delta, \boldsymbol{A}, \boldsymbol{B})\) into the discrete parameters \((\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})\) used by the recurrence. The paper presents it as one choice of discretization rule among several [¶25][¶26].

\[
\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = \exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}), \qquad \overline{\boldsymbol{B}} = (\Delta \boldsymbol{A})^{-1}\left(\exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}) - \boldsymbol{I}\right)\cdot \Delta \boldsymbol{B}
\]

## What it computes

The continuous system is \(h'(t) = \boldsymbol{A}h(t) + \boldsymbol{B}x(t)\), with output \(y(t) = \boldsymbol{C}h(t)\) [¶24]. The model works on sequences, so it needs a step-by-step recurrence \(h_t = \overline{\boldsymbol{A}}h_{t-1} + \overline{\boldsymbol{B}}x_t\) [¶24]. Equation (4) gives the matrices for that recurrence, assuming the input is held constant over each step of length \(\Delta\). This is the standard ZOH assumption, which the paper does not spell out. Under it, \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}\) is the exact state transition across one step, and \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}\) is the exact effect of the input over that step.

The paper calls this the first stage of the SSM computation: discretization is "simply... the first step of the computation graph in the forward pass" [¶27]. Section 2 describes the first stage as mapping \((\Delta, \boldsymbol{A}, \boldsymbol{B}) \to (\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})\) through fixed formulas [¶25].

## What each symbol means

- **\(\Delta\)** is the step size, or timescale. The paper says SSMs can be read as a continuous system discretized by a timestep \(\Delta\) [¶93]. In the selective model, \(\Delta\) is computed from the input [¶56].
- **\(\boldsymbol{A}\)** is the continuous-time state matrix. It is diagonal in the paper [¶33].
- **\(\boldsymbol{B}\)** is the continuous-time input matrix.
- **\(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}\)** and **\(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}\)** are the discrete counterparts that appear in the recurrence (2a) [¶24][¶28].
- **\(\exp(\cdot)\)** is the matrix exponential. For a diagonal \(\boldsymbol{A}\), it applies the scalar exponential to each diagonal entry.
- **\(\boldsymbol{I}\)** is the identity matrix, so \(\exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A}) - \boldsymbol{I}\) has the same shape as \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

## Reading the formulas

- \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = \exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})\) is the decay factor for the state over one step. Because the paper uses negative real or complex-valued diagonal entries of \(\boldsymbol{A}\), the magnitude of \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}\) falls below 1 as \(\Delta\) grows. This is what makes the state forget its past.
- \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}\) scales how much the current input enters the state. The factor \((\Delta\boldsymbol{A})^{-1}(\exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A}) - \boldsymbol{I})\) simplifies to \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}(\exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A}) - \boldsymbol{I})\), which is the integral of \(\exp(\boldsymbol{A}s)\boldsymbol{B}\) over one step. That simplification is my own standard calculus step, not something the paper writes out.

## Why it matters for selectivity

Because \(\Delta\) controls both \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}\) and \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}\), it is the key selective parameter:

- A large \(\Delta\) resets the state and focuses on the current input. A small \(\Delta\) keeps the state and ignores the input [¶93].
- The paper argues that selectivity in \(\Delta\) is enough to make \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}\) and \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}\) selective, which is why \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is left non-selective [¶94].

Theorem 1 shows the ZOH rule recovers an RNN-style gate. With \(N=1\), \(\boldsymbol{A}=-1\), \(\boldsymbol{B}=1\) and \(\Delta = \mathrm{softplus}(\mathrm{Linear}(x_t))\), the rule gives \(\overline{A}_t = 1 - \sigma(\mathrm{Linear}(x_t))\) and \(\overline{B}_t = \sigma(\mathrm{Linear}(x_t))\) [¶362]. Substituting these into the recurrence gives the gated update \(h_t = (1-g_t)h_{t-1} + g_t x_t\) [¶85][¶364]. The paper uses this to argue that discretization is the principled basis for heuristic gating [¶83].

The paper's Appendix C states this derivation, and the scalar check above matches it: with \(\boldsymbol{A}=-1\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}=1\), \(\overline{B} = 1 - \exp(-\Delta)\) [¶362].

runs.question: mamba-figure
runs.text:
**Mamba 1.4B peaks at about 1,814 tokens/s at batch size 128. The best Transformer 1.3B reaches about 364 tokens/s at batch size 32, before it runs out of memory. That peak-to-peak ratio is about 5×, which is where the "5× higher throughput" claim comes from. It compares different batch sizes, though, so it is not a same-batch comparison.**

[[part 1]]

The right panel plots inference throughput (tokens/s) against batch size for Mamba 1.4B, Transformer 1.3B, Mamba 6.9B and Transformer 6.7B, with a prompt length of 2048 [¶163]. Reading the bar labels (small and approximate, since the paper gives no table for this figure):

- **Mamba 1.4B** rises at every batch size: about 140, 247, 441, 744, 1089, 1445, 1688, then 1814 at batch 128.
- **Transformer 1.3B** reaches about 79, 132, 199, 265, 323, then 364 at batch 32. It is marked OOM at batch 64 and 128.

At matched batch sizes the gap is smaller than 5×: about 1.8× at batch 1, 3.4× at batch 16 (1089 vs. 323) and 4.0× at batch 32 (1445 vs. 364). The 5× figure only appears when Mamba's largest batch is set against the Transformer's largest feasible batch.

[[part 2]]

The left panel is the training-side scan benchmark. It is outside the scope of your question, but the caption's "40×" claim refers to it, not to the inference chart.

**Where the claim comes from**

- The Figure 8 caption states "Mamba can achieve 5× higher throughput than Transformers" [¶163]. The text in Section 4.5 says "4-5× higher inference throughput than a Transformer of similar size, since without the KV cache it can use much higher batch sizes" [¶162]. The abstract and introduction also cite 5× [¶4][¶17].
- The benchmark is in Appendix E.5 [¶495–496]. It uses a prompt length of 2048, generates 128 tokens, varies batch size from 1 to 128, and computes throughput as batch size × 128 / time, averaged over three runs on an A100 80GB.
- The paper's explanation is that Mamba has no KV cache, so it can run much larger batches, and Transformers hit memory limits first [¶162].

**Caveats**

- The paper does not state which batch sizes the 5× is computed from. It matches the peak-to-peak comparison, and my reading agrees with that.
- The text says "4-5×" while the caption says "5×". The chart supports roughly 4× at matched batch sizes and about 5× at peak.
- The 6.9B/6.7B pair gives a similar picture: Mamba 6.9B peaks at about 515 tokens/s (batch 128), and Transformer 6.7B peaks at about 120 (batch 16), roughly 4.3×.

runs.question: muon-critical
runs.text:
**Short answer:** No. Theorem 3 proves convergence to an approximate stationary point, not a global minimum. Its rate also does not transfer automatically to the practical capped implementation, which the paper does not analyze.

## Theorem 3 does not prove a global minimum

- The guarantee is a bound on the average of a mixed stationarity measure, \(\frac{1}{T}\sum_t \mathbb{E}[\|P^\top\nabla F(W_t)\|_* + \|Q\nabla F(W_t)\|_F] \le O(T^{-1/4})\) [¶63–¶64]. Small gradients at the iterates are a statement about stationarity, not optimality.
- The setting is stochastic nonconvex optimization. The assumptions are L-smoothness, a finite lower bound, and bounded-variance stochastic gradients [¶24–¶29]. No convexity or other condition that would make stationary points global minima is assumed.
- The bound is an average over iterates, and it contains the initial gap and noise terms (proof, Eq. after [¶298]). It is not a last-iterate guarantee.
- The paper itself describes the result as matching full-space Muon's stationarity rate [¶66].

## The rate does not automatically apply to the practical implementation

Theorem 3 is for Algorithm 3, which uses a fixed orthonormal basis, an exact matrix sign, and the unmodified residual term [¶57–¶60]. The practical variant in Appendix E.2.1 differs in several ways that the theorem does not cover:

1. **Residual cap.** The residual weight is replaced by \(\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}=\min\{\gamma,\rho\sqrt{\|P_kZ_{k,t}\|_F^2/\max\{\|R_{k,t}\|_F^2,\epsilon\}}\}\), which is data-dependent [¶446]. The paper motivates this for early-training instability [¶442] and says the cap guarantees \(\|\widehat{\gamma}R\|_F\le\rho\|PZ\|_F\) [¶477]. The analysis has no such step; its residual weight is the fixed \(\gamma\).
2. **Extra update terms.** The practical update adds a shape-dependent factor \(0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\) and weight decay \(-\eta\lambda W\) [¶444, ¶447]. Neither appears in Algorithm 3 or the proofs.
3. **Approximate basis.** The exact SVD is replaced by a warm-started approximation (QR with row normalization) [¶448–¶450]. Theorem 4 needs an orthonormal basis that is predictable from the prior history (Assumption 4 [¶31]). The paper does not check that the approximate basis satisfies this.
4. **Approximate matrix sign.** The matrix sign is computed with 5 Newton–Schulz iterations [¶459, ¶464]. The proof uses the exact \(\mathrm{msign}\) and its properties (Lemma 1, Lemma 2 [¶253, ¶261–¶265]).
5. **Parameter scaling.** Theorem 3 gives only \(\gamma=\Theta(T^{1/4})\). The constant is unspecified, so the experimental values (for example \(\gamma=8192\), Table 7 [¶456]) cannot be checked against the theorem.

The experiments (Section 6, Appendix E.2) show empirical performance only. They are not a convergence proof for the capped implementation.

**Outside the paper:** I cannot say whether the cap or the approximations would preserve the rate. That would need a separate analysis.

runs.question: muon-detail
runs.text:
Appendix E.2.1 makes two changes to the single-stage PMRC update of Algorithm 4: a **residual cap** on the residual correction, and a **warm-started subspace approximation** that replaces the exact SVD when the basis is refreshed. The timing evidence is a per-matrix latency measurement of the basis refresh on one GPU. The appendix does not report end-to-end training time or how closely the approximate basis matches the exact SVD.

**1. Residual cap**

- **Problem:** A single global \(\gamma\) cannot keep the residual term on the same scale as the projected Muon direction across parameter blocks and steps. Early in training, \(\gamma\lVert(I-P_kP_k^\top)G_{k,t}\rVert_F\) can greatly exceed \(\lVert P_kZ_{k,t}\rVert_F\), and the authors link this imbalance to loss fluctuations early on [¶442].
- **Rule:** The residual weight becomes \(\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}=\min\{\gamma,\ \rho\sqrt{\lVert P_kZ_{k,t}\rVert_F^2/\max\{\lVert R_{k,t}\rVert_F^2,\epsilon\}}\}\), with \(R_{k,t}=(I-P_kP_k^\top)G_{k,t}\) [¶445][¶446]. The update is \(W_{k,t+1}=W_{k,t}-0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\,\eta(P_kZ_{k,t}+\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}R_{k,t})-\eta\lambda W_{k,t}\) [¶444].
- **Guarantee:** By construction, \(\lVert\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}R_{k,t}\rVert_F\le\rho\lVert P_kZ_{k,t}\rVert_F\) [¶477]. The original \(\gamma\) is kept whenever the residual is already below the threshold [¶442].
- **Settings:** \(\rho=4\) and \(\epsilon=10^{-30}\). The shape-dependent scale \(0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\) and weight decay \(\lambda\) are inherited from Liu et al. (2025) [¶447].

**2. Approximate basis refresh**

- **Method:** Given the gradient \(G\) and the previous basis \(P^{\mathrm{prev}}\), the new basis is \(P=\mathrm{QR}(G\,f_{\mathrm{RN}}((P^{\mathrm{prev}})^\top G)^\top)\), where \(f_{\mathrm{RN}}\) is row normalization. The singular values are estimated from the row norms of \(P^\top G\). The QR step uses SCQR [¶448][¶449][¶450]. This is adapted from ARO (Gong et al., 2026) [¶448].
- **Timing evidence:** Table 3 gives per-matrix projector latency on LLaMA-350M shapes on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU. The exact SVD takes about 57–58 ms per matrix, and the approximation takes about 3.0–3.2 ms [¶451][¶452]:

| Matrix shape | Exact SVD (ms) | Approximate (ms) |
|---|---|---|
| 1024×1024 | 58.01 | 3.21 |
| 2736×1024 | 57.75 | 2.98 |
| 1024×2736 | 57.36 | 2.98 |

The appendix does not give an accuracy comparison between the approximate and exact bases.

The appendix does not say what fraction of total training time these refreshes account for. Section 6 states that the practical variant with the residual cap and approximate refresh is the one used in the experiments [¶81].

runs.question: prism-false_premise
runs.text:
CPR accounts for a small share of the drive-insertion gain, not most of it. The premise is also off: CPR does not signal the action expert at test time.

**CPR's share:** In the cumulative ablation on drive insertion (Table 4), success goes from 0.35 for π0.5 to 0.95 for full Prism, a 0.60 gain [¶95]. The steps are:

- **+CPR:** 0.35 to 0.45, +0.10 (about 17% of the gain)
- **+ρ (precision weighting):** 0.45 to 0.70, +0.25 (about 42%)
- **+τ (clean-end emphasis):** 0.70 to 0.85, +0.15 (about 25%)
- **+SNR gating:** 0.85 to 0.95, +0.10 (about 17%)

The paper's text describes the same progression [¶97]. Precision weighting (PSW) gives the largest single step.

**Why CPR isn't a test-time signal:** The auxiliary head is discarded after training, leaving the backbone and standard ODE solver unchanged at inference [¶57]. CPR's job is to shape the VLM condition representation during training [¶71][¶73]. PSW uses the offline PPS label, not the CPR prediction, so the prediction never feeds back into sample weighting [¶57][¶73]. The method adds no inference-time module [¶75].

**Caveats:**
- The ablation is cumulative, so CPR is measured only as the first addition. Its marginal effect when added last is not reported.
- Each success rate is out of 20 trials [¶84], so the CPR step is two trials. The paper reports no variance or repeated runs for the ablation, so treat the split as indicative.
- The paper also notes that CPR alone lowers overall residuals but worsens two lower-demand bins. Adding PSW improves every bin [¶101]. The authors read this as CPR identifying precision-demanding contexts while PSW allocates supervision [¶101].

runs.question: prism-figure_layout
runs.text:
The figure has two halves. Panel (a) on the left is an offline step that turns robot motion into a per-frame precision-demand score, \(\rho\). Panel (b) on the right is the training setup, where that score is used in two places: to reweight the flow-matching loss (PSW) and as a regression target for the VLM's features (CPR). Inference is unchanged, and the CPR head is discarded after training [¶54][¶57].

[[part 1]]
**Trajectory-derived signals (panel a, top).** Three cues come from the demonstrated robot motion: joint motion, end-effector motion, and gripper engagement, each plotted against time \(t\). The arrows show joint and end-effector motion feeding a "relative slowness" cue, and gripper engagement feeding a "motion validity" cue. The text defines these from joint and end-effector displacements, percentile-ranked slowness within an episode, and gripper engagement [¶59][¶60][¶61]. No camera images are used as PPS inputs [¶158].

[[part 2]]
**PPS and the demand strips (panel a, middle and bottom).** The PPS box combines those cues into a precision-demand score \(\rho\) in [0,1], computed as \(\rho_i = g_i^{\mathrm{eng}}\,\mathrm{slow}_i\,t_i\) and then smoothed and clipped [¶61][¶62]. The output is drawn as colour strips under sample frames, using the Low-to-High scale at the bottom. The first strip is mostly low-to-mid teal. The second has orange and red bands during the handover and insertion portion, which marks higher demand. The label is fixed before training begins [¶57].

[[part 3]]
**VLM and action expert (panel b, top).** The vision encoder takes the camera views, and the language instruction and discretized state are tokenized into the same prefix. The Vision Language Model processes this prefix, and the action expert denoises a noisy action chunk, shown as the dashed trajectory [¶18][¶54]. The bottom row of VLM output squares is the set of prefix hidden states that CPR reads. The action expert's flow-matching loss is what PSW reweights.

[[part 4]]
**Conditional Precision Regularization (CPR, panel b, bottom left).** The prefix hidden states are combined by mask-aware mean pooling, using the padding mask (1 for valid tokens, 0 for padding), into a pooled condition feature. A small predictor (Linear, SiLU, Linear, Sigmoid) outputs a predicted demand \(\hat{\rho}\). A precision regression loss compares \(\hat{\rho}\) with the offline \(\rho\) strips. The loss is the squared error \((\hat{\rho}-\rho)^2\) [¶71][¶72]. The predictor is a 256-wide MLP [¶156]. The gradient from this loss shapes the VLM representation itself [¶73].

[[part 5]]
**Precision-Scaled Weighting (PSW, panel b, bottom right).** The ground-truth action chunk gives an action RMS, which feeds a flow-time visibility term \(\Psi\) together with the sampled flow time. The visibility term is \(\Psi_i=(1-\tau_i)^{p}\bigl(1-e^{-\mathrm{SNR}_i/\tau_0}\bigr)\) [¶66]. The precision-weighting block combines \(\Psi\) with the offline \(\rho\) into the weight \(w_i = 1+\gamma\rho_i\Psi_i\), which lies in \([1,1+\gamma]\) [¶66][¶67]. This weight multiplies the flow-matching loss \(L_{FM}\) for the output action, giving the precision-weighted loss [¶68].

**How the pieces connect.** The offline \(\rho\) from panel (a) feeds two branches: it is the target for CPR, and it is the multiplier inside PSW's weight. The predicted \(\hat{\rho}\) goes only to the CPR loss and does not feed back into the weights [¶57][¶73]. The two losses are summed as \(\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PSW}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{CPR}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR}}\) [¶74]. The figure's "Combined Training Objective" box represents this sum, though the figure does not show the weights or the formula. The paper uses \(\lambda_{\mathrm{CPR}}=0.1\) for the insertion setting [¶87].

runs.question: apertus-detail_deep
runs.text:
The main RL run used a learning rate of \(1\times 10^{-6}\), asymmetric clipping of \((0.2, 0.28)\), and **no KL penalty**.

- **Learning rate:** AdamW at \(1\times 10^{-6}\) [¶702]. The 8B run took 480 steps and the 70B run took 180 [¶702, ¶211].
- **Clipping:** Asymmetric clipping with bounds (0.2, 0.28) [¶702]. Appendix G also lists a geometric-mean loss aggregation and leave-one-out advantage estimation [¶702].
- **KL penalty:** None. Appendix G states "no KL penalty" [¶702].

Don't confuse these with the separate RL ablation in Section 4.7 (Table 12). That ablation used a constant learning rate of \(2\times 10^{-6}\), DAPO asymmetric clipping, and no KL penalty, with 200 GRPO steps per prompt set [¶257]. It was a controlled comparison, not the run that produced the released models.

runs.question: apertus-explain
runs.text:
Apertus 1.5 keeps the same text transformer and adds images and audio as extra tokens. The model reads them as sequences of discrete codes, and the training happens in three phases: continued pretraining, long-context extension, and post-training.

**1. Turn images and audio into tokens**

- Images go through the Emu3.5 tokenizer. Each 16×16 pixel block becomes one code from a 131,072-entry codebook, so a 512×512 image is 1,024 tokens ([¶45]–[¶47]).
- Audio goes through the WavTokenizer codec, which emits one code per 600 samples. That is 40 tokens per second, or 2,400 tokens per minute ([¶50]–[¶51]).
- These codes are appended to the existing text vocabulary, giving 266,440 entries ([¶43]). Because the codes are just more token IDs, the transformer needs no image or audio encoder ([¶40], [¶87]).

**2. Continued pretraining in three stages**

The starting point is the Apertus 1.0 checkpoints. Their text is preserved and the architecture is unchanged ([¶107], [¶123]).

- **Stage 1 (unpaired data):** The model sees text, plus images and audio with no captions. It learns to predict tokens of every modality. The loss covers all of them ([¶125], Table 2).
- **Stage 2 (paired data):** Image-caption and audio-transcript pairs are added to text. The loss now covers only text, so the model learns to relate the new inputs to language without being trained to generate images or audio ([¶124], [¶125]).
- **Stage 3 (cooldown):** Higher-quality and reasoning-heavy text is emphasized, with some paired speech and a small amount of instruction data. The loss is again text-only ([¶125], [¶128]).

Token budgets are in Table 3: about 4.0T tokens for the 8B and about 2.0T for the 70B. Text is roughly 55–60% of the mix ([¶54]). The 70B run stopped before consuming its full multimodal mixture ([¶144]).

The two-stage split rests on a controlled study. Giving image and text tokens equal loss weight during alignment hurt image understanding, and text-only targets worked best ([¶105]).

**3. Long-context extension**

After the three stages, the context window grows from 8K to 32K, 65K, 131K, and finally 262K tokens. Each step starts from the previous checkpoint, and the rotary position base is adjusted ([¶131]–[¶133]).

**4. Post-training**

- **SFT:** About 3.7M text samples plus image and audio data. Placeholder tokens such as `<|image|>` and `<|audio|>` mark where media goes in a user message ([¶153], [¶158]–[¶169]).
- **Thinking mode:** Reasoning traces sit between delimiter tokens. Thinking is a flag of the chat template, not a separate model ([¶155]).
- **Long-context SFT:** At 262K tokens, this restores retrieval that short-context SFT had degraded. RULER at 262K fell from 54.8 to 8.3 after SFT ([¶191]).
- **RL with verifiable rewards:** Math, instruction-following, and code answers are checked automatically ([¶209]–[¶211]).
- **Preference alignment:** Offline and online DPO use a judge model. The 8B uses online DPO alone; the 70B adds an offline DPO stage first ([¶219]–[¶226]).
- **Charter alignment (SDPO):** Applied to the 8B only. The 70B ships the DPO checkpoint ([¶231]).

**Main trade-off**

Adding modalities initially hurt text ability. The text loss crept upward in Stage 1, then recovered during the Stage 3 cooldown ([¶141]). The paper attributes most of this to re-warming the learning rate, not to the new data itself ([¶141]).

runs.question: apertus-synthesis
runs.text:
The drop was about 46.5 points, and the released 8B did not fully recover. At 256K it reaches 50.5 against a pre-SFT 54.8, a gap of about 4.3 points.

**The drop.** After SFT at 16,384 tokens, RULER at 262,144 tokens fell from 54.8 to 8.3 for Apertus 1.5 8B, while short-context scores were unaffected [¶191]. The paper attributes this to short-context SFT biasing attention toward local patterns [¶191].

**The fix.** The authors added a dedicated long-context SFT stage at the full 262,144-token length, following the staged recipes of Qwen 2.5 and Nemotron 3 Nano Omni [¶191]. It kept the production SFT learning rate, held constant at 6×10⁻⁵ for the 8B, with 195 warmup steps and a global batch size of 32 sequences [¶191]. They then evaluated checkpoints across context lengths and carried the best one into RL [¶191]. Section 4.3 describes the data mixture [¶193].

**Recovery across the pipeline** (RULER at 256K, Table 36 [¶330]):

| Checkpoint | 256K score |
|---|---|
| Base (pre-SFT, long-context pretrained) | 54.8 |
| After SFT | 8.3 |
| After long-context SFT | 44.9 |
| After RL | 48.8 |
| After DPO | 50.4 |
| After SDPO (released 8B) | 50.5 |

The released 8B includes SDPO [¶231], so 50.5 is its final score. Long-context SFT recovers most of the loss, and RL and preference optimization add further gains even though neither trains on long documents [¶329].

**Other context lengths.** The final 8B is at or above its base at shorter lengths (8K: 87.4 vs 85.9), and close at 128K (61.1 vs 61.5) [¶330]. The gap is concentrated at 256K.

**The 70B** did not fully recover either. Its base scored 51.0 at 256K, and its final DPO checkpoint scored 45.6 [¶330]. The paper does not give a 70B SDPO row.
