runs.question: apertus-synthesis
runs.text:
**Short answer:** ordinary SFT at 16K context collapsed RULER at the full 262,144-token context from **54.8 to 8.3** on the 8B. A dedicated long-context SFT stage trained at the full 262K sequence length mostly repaired it, and later stages added a bit more — but the released 8B ends at **50.5 at 256K**, i.e. close to but not quite back to its pre-SFT 54.8 [¶191][¶330].

**The drop.** After production SFT at a 16,384-token sequence length, the RULER score of Apertus 1.5 8B at 262,144 tokens fell from 54.8 to 8.3, while short-context scores were unaffected. The paper attributes this to short-context SFT systematically biasing attention toward local patterns, degrading the long-range retrieval established during context extension (Section 4.3) [¶191]. Table 36 shows the same collapse on HELMET (256K not measured there; at 128K HELMET fell to 8.7 post-SFT vs 36.5 for the base) [¶330].

**The fix.** A dedicated long-context SFT stage at the full 262,144-token sequence length, following the staged recipes of Qwen 2.5 and Nemotron 3 Nano Omni: each model keeps its production SFT learning rate held constant (\(6\times 10^{-5}\) for the 8B, after 195 warmup steps, global batch size 32), and once the stage finishes, checkpoints are evaluated across context lengths and the best one is carried into RL [¶191]. Its data mixture is 30.3% long-context multimodal, 63.2% short-context multimodal, 5.4% short-context text, 1.0% long-context text by token count (Section 4.3, Table 8) [¶193]. RL and DPO then add further RULER gains even though neither trains on long documents [¶330][¶145].

**Recovery at 256K (RULER, Apertus 1.5 8B, Table 36) [¶330]:**

| Checkpoint | 128k | 256k |
|---|---|---|
| Base (pre-SFT) | 61.5 | 54.8 |
| after SFT | 18.9 | 8.3 |
| after long-context SFT | 59.5 | 44.9 |
| after RL | 60.1 | 48.8 |
| after DPO | 61.5 | 50.4 |
| released (after SDPO) | 61.1 | **50.5** |

So: **no, the released 8B does not fully regain its pre-SFT score at the extreme end.** At 128K and below it effectively recovers (61.1 vs 61.5 at 128K; it actually exceeds the base at 64K and below), but at 256K it remains about 4.3 points short of the base model's 54.8 [¶330].

runs.question: apertus-unanswerable
runs.text:
**Short answer: the paper does not report a dollar cost or a CO₂ figure at all.** It only reports compute time and energy. Any dollar or tonnage number would come from outside assumptions, not from the report.

What the paper does give (Section 6.3, Table 40):

- **Logged production training segments**: roughly 225,000 GPU-hours for the 8B continued-pretraining stages plus 1.50 million for the 70B stages, plus the long-context extensions — together about **2 million GPU-hours ≈ 1.1 GWh** [¶370].
- **Whole project allocation**: 9 million GPU-hours over the project duration, translating to an estimated **~5 GWh** — but this excludes idle time and covers other Swiss AI Initiative projects too [¶370].
- **Method caveat**: energy is estimated from measured GPU-hours times an assumed 560 W per GH200 module (below the 660 W cap), and the estimate covers only logged segments — it excludes post-training, evaluation, ablations, and idle reservation time [¶370].
- **Carbon**: the report states that Alps draws on carbon-free hydropower and uses closed-cycle lake-water cooling [¶370], which is why no CO₂ tonnage is claimed.

**On cost**: nowhere in the report is a training cost in dollars (or any currency) given. You could only derive a rough proxy from GPU-hours and an assumed cloud price per GH200-hour — e.g., 2 million GPU-hours × some price per GPU-hour — but the paper itself offers no such figure, and the allocation was an in-kind supercomputing reservation rather than a purchased cloud run [¶361], so a market-price estimate would be misleading.

If you want, I can lay out the energy numbers as a small breakdown table.

runs.question: dpo-derivation
runs.text:
The gradient follows from one application of the chain rule plus two sigmoid identities. Here is the derivation, per preference triple \((x, y_w, y_l)\).

## Setup

The per-example loss from Eq. 7 [¶33] is

\[
\ell(\theta) = -\log\sigma(\Delta), \qquad
\Delta := \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)} = \hat r_\theta(x,y_w) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_l),
\]

where \(\hat r_\theta(x,y) = \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}\) is exactly the implicit reward defined in Section 4 [¶37].

## Steps

**1. Chain rule.** Only the composite \(\Delta\) depends on \(\theta\), so

\[
\nabla_\theta \ell = -\frac{\sigma'(\Delta)}{\sigma(\Delta)}\,\nabla_\theta \Delta .
\]

This is the structure of Eq. (22) in Appendix A.4 [¶171], with \(u = \Delta\).

**2. Sigmoid identities.** Using \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\) and \(1-\sigma(z) = \sigma(-z)\),

\[
\frac{\sigma'(\Delta)}{\sigma(\Delta)} = 1 - \sigma(\Delta) = \sigma(-\Delta).
\]

This is where the \(\sigma\) weight comes from: it is not in the loss, it is the derivative of the \(\log\sigma\).

**3. Gradient of \(\Delta\).** The reference model \(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is a fixed (detached) copy, so its log-probabilities are constants and only the policy terms survive:

\[
\nabla_\theta \Delta = \beta\Big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x) - \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)\Big].
\]

**4. Combine and rewrite the weight.** Since \(-\Delta = \hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\),

\[
\nabla_\theta \ell = -\beta\,\underbrace{\sigma\big(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\big)}_{\text{higher weight when reward estimate is wrong}}\Big[\underbrace{\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}_{\text{increase } y_w} - \underbrace{\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}_{\text{decrease } y_l}\Big],
\]

which is precisely the boxed gradient in Section 4 [¶37]; averaging over \((x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}\) and scaling by \(-\beta\) gives the full expression there. The appendix version [¶173] is the same computation carried through Eq. (21)–(22) [¶169][¶171].

## What the weight does

- If the implicit reward already ranks \(y_w\) above \(y_l\), then \(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w) < 0\), the sigmoid is near 0, and the pair is barely updated.
- If the model ranks \(y_l\) above \(y_w\), the weight approaches 1 and the example gets full force.

That dynamic per-example weighting is what distinguishes DPO from a naive probability-ratio / unlikelihood objective, and the paper reports that dropping it causes model degeneration [¶38], with degenerate unlikelihood samples shown in Table 3 [¶219].

Implementation-wise, the code in Appendix B [¶200] is exactly this: `-F.logsigmoid(beta * (pi_logratios - ref_logratios))`, and it returns the detached implicit rewards `beta * (pi_logps - ref_logps)`.

## One small caveat

Appendix Eq. (21) [¶169] writes the sigmoid argument as \(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l)} - \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w)}\), i.e. with the sign of \(u\) reversed relative to Eq. 7. Read literally that would define \(u=-\Delta\); the final gradient in [¶173] nonetheless matches the derivation above from Eq. 7, so it appears to be a sign typo in that intermediate line rather than a substantive difference.

runs.question: dpo-detail
runs.text:
For the Reddit TL;DR summarization run specifically, the settings are **β = 0.5**, with everything else at their defaults [¶201]:

| Hyperparameter | TL;DR summarization value |
|---|---|
| β (KL penalty strength) | 0.5 |
| Optimizer | RMSprop |
| Learning rate | 1e-6 |
| Batch size | 64 |
| LR schedule | Linear warmup from 0 to 1e-6 over 150 steps |

These come from Appendix B (Implementation Details and Hyperparameters). The paper states: "Unless noted otherwise, we use a β = 0.1, batch size of 64 and the RMSprop optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-6 by default... For TL;DR summarization, we use β = 0.5, while rest of the parameters remain the same" [¶201].

A few reproduction notes worth knowing:

- The **reference model** is a GPT-J SFT model fine-tuned on human-written TL;DR summaries (the CarperAI/openai_summarize_tldr_sft checkpoint) [¶58][¶272], and π_ref is initialized to π^SFT since the preference data was sampled from a similarly-trained SFT model [¶38].
- The **preference data** is the Stiennon et al. human preference dataset over Reddit TL;DR samples [¶58].
- The paper notes it "did not meaningfully tune DPO's β" for this task, so the reported ~61% win rate at temperature 0 may underestimate DPO's potential [¶67].
- PyTorch reference code for the loss is given in Appendix B [¶200], and further experimental details (e.g., generation/evaluation setup) are in Appendix C [¶202].

One caveat: the paper doesn't report things like number of training epochs/steps, sequence length, or weight decay for the TL;DR run, so those would have to come from the released code rather than the paper itself.

runs.question: dpo-figure
runs.text:
Looking at the left panel of Figure 3 [¶60], the caption's claim is not quite what the plot shows — **Best of 128 also sits above the 50% line at every temperature tested**. The caption is best read as "the only *computationally efficient* method," which matches the text in Section 6.2 [¶68].

Here's the temperature-by-temperature comparison (win rate vs. the chosen response in the Anthropic-HH test set, dashed line = 0.5 parity):

| Sampling temp | DPO (yellow) | Best of 128 (green) | Winner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | ~0.37 | ~0.54 | **Best of 128**, clearly (error bars don't overlap) |
| 0.7 | ~0.60 | ~0.59 | Roughly tied (overlapping error bars) |
| 1.0 | ~0.63 | ~0.61 | DPO slightly higher, but error bars overlap |

Key observations:

- **At low temperature, DPO underperforms badly** (~37% win rate at temp 0.25, below parity), while Best of 128 is comfortably above 0.5 even there. DPO only becomes competitive at higher sampling temperatures.
- The two methods are statistically indistinguishable at temps 0.7 and 1.0, with DPO having a small edge at 1.0.
- Preferred-FT (magenta, peaks ~0.42) and the Pythia-2.8B base (teal, ~0.15–0.25) never reach parity, so *among the cheap methods* DPO is indeed the only one that beats the chosen completions [¶68].

So the honest summary: the plot shows DPO matching the far more expensive Best of 128 baseline (which samples 128 completions per query at test time) at its best temperatures, but Best of 128 is also above 50% — and is actually better than DPO at temperature 0.25. The caption's "only method" phrasing only holds once you add the qualifier about computational efficiency that appears in the body text [¶68], where the authors also note they treat Best of 128 as a rough proxy for PPO-level performance.

runs.question: dpo-visual
runs.text:
Here is one DPO training step on a single preference pair \((x, y_w, y_l)\), drawn from Eq. (7) and the gradient analysis in Section 4.

**What happens per pair:**

1. **Data.** Take one triple \((x, y_w, y_l)\) from the offline preference dataset \(\mathcal{D}\) [¶38].
2. **Two forward passes.** Score both completions with the trainable policy \(\pi_\theta\) and with the frozen reference \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) (initialized to \(\pi^{\mathrm{SFT}}\) when available [¶38]). This gives four log-probabilities; no sampling is needed during training [¶4].
3. **Implicit rewards.** Define \(\hat{r}_\theta(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)}\) [¶37].
4. **Loss.** Plug the reward gap into the Bradley-Terry cross-entropy [Eq. (7)]() [¶33]:

\[
\mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma\!\left(\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_w) - \hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l)\right)
= -\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}\right)
\]

5. **Backprop.** The gradient \(-\beta\,\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\,[\nabla_\theta \log \pi(y_w\mid x) - \nabla_\theta \log \pi(y_l\mid x)]\) raises the likelihood of \(y_w\), lowers that of \(y_l\), and weights each pair by how wrongly the implicit reward currently ranks it [¶37]. This weight is what distinguishes DPO from a naive probability-ratio objective, whose unweighted version degenerates (Appendix Table 3 [¶219]). Only \(\theta\) updates; \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) stays fixed. In code the step is a single `logsigmoid` call (Appendix B [¶200]).

input.title: One DPO training step on a preference pair
input.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    D["Preference pair: prompt x, chosen y_w, rejected y_l"]
    D --> P["Policy pi_theta: log pi_theta(y_w|x), log pi_theta(y_l|x)"]
    D --> R["Frozen ref pi_ref: log pi_ref(y_w|x), log pi_ref(y_l|x)"]
    P --> RR["Implicit reward r_hat(y) = beta * (log pi_theta(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x))"]
    R --> RR
    RR --> GAP["Reward gap u = r_hat(y_w) - r_hat(y_l)"]
    GAP --> LOSS["Loss = -log sigmoid(u)"]
    W["Weight = sigma(-u): high when pair is misordered"]
    GAP --> W
    LOSS --> GRAD["Grad = -beta * weight * [grad log pi(y_w) - grad log pi(y_l)]"]
    W --> GRAD
    GRAD --> UPD["Update pi_theta only; pi_ref stays frozen"]
    UPD -.-> P

runs.question: mamba-equation
runs.text:
## What Eq. (4) computes

Equation (4) is the **discretization step** of a structured state space model — it converts the parameters of a continuous-time system into the parameters of the discrete recurrence the model actually runs [¶25][¶26]. It implements the **zero-order hold (ZOH)** rule, one of several possible discretization rules \((f_A, f_B)\) [¶25].

The formulas are:

\[
\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = \exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}), \qquad
\overline{\boldsymbol{B}} = (\Delta \boldsymbol{A})^{-1}(\exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}) - \boldsymbol{I}) \cdot \Delta \boldsymbol{B}
\]

## Symbol by symbol

- \(\boldsymbol{A}\): the continuous-time state matrix, \(\boldsymbol{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\), governing how the latent state evolves. In practice it is structured as diagonal, so it is represented by just \(N\) numbers [¶33][¶34].
- \(\boldsymbol{B}\): the continuous-time input matrix, \(\boldsymbol{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}\), which maps the scalar input \(x(t)\) into the latent state [¶34].
- \(\Delta\): the discretization timestep (a scalar per channel in the SSM parameterization), which sets the resolution at which the continuous system is sampled [¶25][¶27]. In Mamba it becomes input-dependent and acts like an RNN gate: large \(\Delta\) resets the state and focuses on the current input, small \(\Delta\) preserves the state and ignores the input [¶93].
- \(\exp(\cdot)\): matrix exponential, used here so that \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = \exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A})\) is the state-transition matrix over one step.
- \(\boldsymbol{I}\): the identity matrix (of size \(N \times N\)).
- \((\Delta \boldsymbol{A})^{-1}\): the inverse of \(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}\), appearing in the ZOH integral of the input over one timestep.
- \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}\), \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}\): the resulting **discrete** parameters that drive the recurrence
  \[
  h_t = \overline{\boldsymbol{A}} h_{t-1} + \overline{\boldsymbol{B}} x_t
  \]
  [¶24].

## Where it fits in the computation

The SSM maps \(x(t) \mapsto y(t)\) through a latent state \(h(t) \in \mathbb{R}^N\) via \(h'(t) = \boldsymbol{A}h(t) + \boldsymbol{B}x(t)\), \(y(t) = \boldsymbol{C}h(t)\) (Eqs. 1a–1b) [¶23][¶24]. Equation (4) is the first stage of the forward pass: it transforms \((\Delta, \boldsymbol{A}, \boldsymbol{B}) \mapsto (\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})\), after which the model can be computed either as the linear recurrence (Eq. 2) or as a global convolution (Eq. 3) [¶28].

Two further points from the paper:

- Discretization connects the model to continuous-time systems and gives properties like resolution invariance and proper normalization; it also connects to RNN gating [¶27]. Theorem 1 uses exactly this ZOH formula to show that with \(N=1\), \(\boldsymbol{A}=-1\), \(\boldsymbol{B}=1\), the selective SSM reduces to a gated RNN update \(h_t = (1-g_t)h_{t-1} + g_t x_t\) [¶84][¶362].
- Alternative SSM flavors can skip discretization entirely and parameterize \((\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})\) directly [¶27].

One caveat worth noting: in the paper's rendered text the ZOH expression appears as written above; the term \((\Delta \boldsymbol{A})^{-1}(\exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}) - \boldsymbol{I})\) is the standard closed-form ZOH input integral. When \(\Delta\) becomes input-dependent (as in Mamba's selection mechanism), this discretization is applied per timestep to get \(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}_t, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_t\), which is why the model is no longer time-invariant and loses the convolutional form [¶55].

runs.question: mamba-figure
runs.text:
**At batch size 128 (the largest shown), Mamba 1.4B reaches 1,814 tokens/s, versus a best of 344 tokens/s for the Transformer 1.3B (achieved at batch size 32 — it goes OOM at batches 64 and 128). That is a ratio of \(1814/344 \approx 5.3\times\), which is where the "5× higher throughput" claim comes from** [¶163]. Note this compares each model at its own largest feasible batch size, not at equal batch size; at batch 32 both are measured and Mamba's lead is about \(1445/344 \approx 4.2\times\).

Overall, the figure benchmarks the selective-SSM scan and end-to-end inference on an A100 80GB PCIe GPU [¶163], supporting the efficiency claims of Section 4.5 [¶162].

[[part 1]] **Training-time panel (left):** "Scan vs Convolution vs Attention time", log-scale time in ms vs sequence length 512 to 512K. The fused selective scan (red, "Scan (ours)") is nearly linear and becomes faster than FlashAttention-2 (blue) beyond roughly 2K–4K sequence length, reaching ~512K without running out of memory. The plain PyTorch scan (green) is roughly 40× slower than the fused one and hits OOM at 128K; the FFT convolution (orange) sits in between and hits OOM at 256K. This matches the text: faster than FlashAttention-2 beyond length 2K and 20–40× faster than a standard scan [¶162], with the speedup coming from fusing discretization + scan + output multiply in SRAM [¶373].

[[part 2]] **Inference-throughput panel (right):** bars of tokens/s vs batch size (1 to 128) with prompt length 2048. Mamba 1.4B (blue) scales almost linearly with batch size: 140, 267, 441, 744, 1,089, 1,445, 1,684, 1,814. Transformer 1.3B (orange) saturates early — 79, 122, 193, 265, 323, 344 — then goes OOM at batches 64 and 128 because of its KV cache. The larger pair shows the same pattern: Mamba 6.9B (green) keeps climbing to 515 tokens/s at batch 128, while Transformer 6.7B (red) flattens and is OOM at 64 and 128. This is why the paper can say an untrained Mamba-6.9B has higher throughput than a 5× smaller Transformer-1.3B [¶162]: 515 > 344. The reason is that as a recurrent model Mamba has no KV cache, so it can use much larger batch sizes [¶162].

runs.question: muon-critical
runs.text:
No to both.

## What Theorem 3 actually guarantees

Theorem 3 proves convergence to a **stationary point**, not a global minimum. Its bound is

\[
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\big[\|P^{\top}\nabla F(W_{t})\|_{*}+\|Q\nabla F(W_{t})\|_{F}\big]\leq O(T^{-1/4})
\]

where \(Q=I-PP^{\top}\) [¶63][¶64]. This is a first-order stationarity measure: it says the average (mixed-norm) gradient shrinks at rate \(O(T^{-1/4})\). Nothing about the loss value approaching \(F_*=\inf_W F(W)\). The setting is stochastic nonconvex optimization under smoothness, lower boundedness and unbiased bounded-variance gradients (Assumptions 1–3) [¶24][¶26][¶28], where global optimality is not attainable in general. Remark 5 only strengthens the *measure*: the mixed quantity upper-bounds \(\|\nabla F(W_t)\|_F\), so Frobenius-norm stationarity follows too [¶68] — still stationarity. Interestingly, the stronger squared-gradient statement \(\frac{1}{T}\sum_t \mathbb{E}[\|\nabla F(W_t)\|_F^2]\le O(T^{-1/2})\) is proved in the appendix [¶300], but that is also just stationarity.

## Why the rate does not transfer to the practical implementation

The theory covers **Algorithm 3** exactly [¶57]: update \(W_{t+1}=W_{t}-\eta(P\,\mathrm{msign}(M_t)+\gamma QG_t)\), fixed orthonormal \(P\), residual weight \(\gamma=\Theta(T^{1/4})\), step \(\eta=\Theta(T^{-3/4})\), \(\beta=\Theta(T^{-1/2})\) [¶63]. The practical variant used in all LLM experiments changes the update in several ways (Appendix E.2.1):

- A **residual cap** \(\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}=\min\{\gamma,\rho\sqrt{\|P_kZ_{k,t}\|_F^2/\max\{\|R_{k,t}\|_F^2,\epsilon\}}\}\) replaces the fixed \(\gamma\) [¶445][¶446], so the residual term is no longer the constant-weight \(\gamma QG_t\) the proof assumes;
- A shape-dependent scaling \(0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\) and **weight decay** \(-\eta\lambda W_{k,t}\) are added [¶444], neither of which appears in Algorithm 3;
- The basis is refreshed by a **warm-started QR approximation** rather than exact SVD [¶448][¶449], and it is refreshed periodically (multi-stage, Algorithm 4) with momentum reinitialization [¶73];
- \(\gamma\) is grid-searched as a large constant (e.g. \(8192\), \(16384\)) [¶456][¶465], not set to \(\Theta(T^{1/4})\) with \(\eta=\Theta(T^{-3/4})\).

The paper is explicit that these are practical modifications motivated by observed loss fluctuations and runtime cost [¶442][¶447][¶452], and it never claims a convergence result for the capped variant. The closest theoretical coverage is Theorem 4 for multi-stage PMRC [¶75], which still assumes the unmodified update and a predictable orthonormal \(P_k\) (Assumption 4) [¶31].

**Bottom line:** the \(O(T^{-1/4})\) result is a stationarity guarantee for the idealized algorithms (1–4), and the empirical gains of the capped, weight-decayed, approximate-SVD implementation rest on the experiments (Tables 1, 2, 8, 9), not on a theorem. Whether the residual cap preserves the rate is, as far as this paper goes, unverified.

runs.question: muon-detail
runs.text:
Appendix E.2.1 modifies Algorithm 4 in two ways [¶441].

## 1. Residual cap (stability)

A single global \(\gamma\) cannot keep the residual correction \(\gamma\|(I-P_kP_k^\top)G_{k,t}\|_F\) aligned with the projected Muon term \(\|P_kZ_{k,t}\|_F\) across blocks and steps. Early in training, when the initial subspace captures little of the gradient, the residual can dominate and this imbalance coincides with loss fluctuations [¶442]. The fix clips the effective residual weight per matrix per step:

\[ W_{k,t+1}=W_{k,t}-0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\,\eta\big(P_kZ_{k,t}+\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}R_{k,t}\big)-\eta\lambda W_{k,t},\qquad R_{k,t}=(I-P_kP_k^\top)G_{k,t} \]

\[ \widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}=\min\left\{\gamma,\ \rho\sqrt{\frac{\|P_kZ_{k,t}\|_F^{2}}{\max\{\|R_{k,t}\|_F^{2},\epsilon\}}}\right\} \]

so that \(\|\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}R_{k,t}\|_F\le\rho\|P_kZ_{k,t}\|_F\), while \(\gamma\) is kept whenever the residual is already below the threshold [¶443][¶445][¶476]. The update also inherits the standard practical Muon shape scaling \(0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\) and weight decay \(\lambda\) from Liu et al. (2025). Settings: \(\rho=4\), \(\epsilon=10^{-30}\) [¶447].

## 2. Approximate basis refresh (speed)

Exact SVD at each refresh is a time bottleneck, so it is replaced by a warm-started subspace approximation adapted from ARO [¶448]:

\[ P=\operatorname{QR}\!\big(G\, f_{\mathrm{RN}}((P^{\mathrm{prev}})^{\top}G)^{\top}\big) \]

where \(f_{\mathrm{RN}}\) row-normalizes and QR returns an orthonormal basis (computed with SCQR); singular values are estimated from the row norms of \(P^\top G\) [¶449][¶450].

## Timing evidence

Table 3 [¶451] reports per-matrix projector latency on LLaMA-350M matrix shapes on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000:

| Shape | Exact SVD | Approx. ("Ours") |
|---|---|---|
| \(1024\times1024\) | 58.01 ms | 3.21 ms |
| \(2736\times1024\) | 57.75 ms | 2.98 ms |
| \(1024\times2736\) | 57.36 ms | 2.98 ms |

i.e. roughly 3 ms versus nearly 58 ms per refresh — about a 19× speedup [¶452].

Related but outside E.2.1: the ablations fix \(\rho=4\) [¶471], and the SFT experiments grid-search \(\gamma\in\{2000,4000,8000,16000\}\) with the cap ratio 4 [¶465].

runs.question: prism-false_premise
runs.text:
The premise doesn't hold: CPR never signals anything at test time. The CPR head and its labels are **discarded after training**, and the architecture, inference procedure, and ODE solver are unchanged — CPR's role is to shape the VLM's *condition representation* during training so precision-demanding contexts are recognizable, not to gate the action expert at inference [¶57][¶73][¶11]. Section 4.5 also reports no mechanism whereby CPR's prediction influences sample weighting: PSW uses the offline label \(\rho_i\), not \(\hat{\rho}\) [¶73].

**CPR contributes the smallest share of the drive-insertion gain.** From the cumulative ablation (Table 4) [¶95]:

| Addition | Success | Marginal gain |
|---|---|---|
| \(\pi_{0.5}\) base | 0.35 | — |
| + CPR | 0.45 | +0.10 |
| + \(\rho\) (precision weighting) | 0.70 | +0.25 |
| + \(\tau\) (clean-end emphasis) | 0.85 | +0.15 |
| + SNR (full Prism) | 0.95 | +0.10 |

Total improvement is \(0.95 - 0.35 = 0.60\), so CPR accounts for **+0.10, about one-sixth of the total gain** — not most of it. The largest single step is precision weighting (+0.25).

Two supporting points from the paper:

- **CPR alone is even slightly harmful in places.** The mechanism analysis shows CPR lowers overall residuals but *worsens* two lower-demand bins; only with PSW do all bins improve. The authors conclude the two are complementary: CPR identifies precision-demanding contexts, PSW allocates supervision by demand and action visibility [¶101].
- **The test-time robustness evidence is about CPR's representation, not a signal.** Removing VLM state inputs leaves Prism at 0.95 success, and Prism still lifts \(\pi_0\) (state to action expert) from 0.25 to 0.80 — showing CPR learns demand from visual-language features [¶103][¶96].

So the supervision-reallocation machinery (PSW's \(\rho\), \(\tau\), and SNR terms) carries roughly five-sixths of the insertion gain, with CPR acting as a representation-level complement [¶101].

runs.question: prism-figure_layout
runs.text:
Figure 3 [¶54] is the full Prism recipe in one picture, split into its two stages: the left panel (a) is **offline precision estimation** — a label computed from raw trajectories before any training — and the right panel (b) is **precision forcing during VLA training** — the two losses that consume that label. The key connection is that the offline score \(\rho\) (the colour bar in (a)) is the shared signal that feeds both the CPR head and the PSW loss weight in (b); nothing in (b) changes the architecture or the inference path, which is why the top-right block (VLM + action expert) looks like an ordinary VLA.

[[part 1]]
Panel (a), inputs: three task stages of drive connector insertion (cable pickup, bimanual handover, connector insertion) run left to right along the time arrow. Below them, the "trajectory-derived signals" box extracts three proprioceptive cues: joint motion and end-effector motion (fed into "relative slowness") and gripper engagement (fed into "motion validity"). These match the PPS ingredients of Section 3.2: \(\Delta q_i\), \(\Delta e_i\) [¶60] and the engagement and gating terms \(g_i^{\mathrm{eng}}, t_i\) [¶61].

[[part 2]]
Panel (a), output: the PPS block fuses those cues into a frame-level **offline precision demand \(\rho\)**. The figure shows two example frames with colour strips underneath, read against the Low-to-High colour bar at the bottom: cool blue over coarse transport, warming to green/yellow over fine interaction. Note the timing — \(\rho\) is fixed before optimization, so it is a label, not a learned quantity [¶57].

[[part 3]]
The conditioning path of the policy: images go through a Vision Encoder, joined by a language instruction ("Insert the cable into the motor drive.") and a discretized state block, whose token embeddings (pink, blue, teal squares) feed the Vision Language Model. The VLM's output prefix tokens condition the Action Expert, which denoises a Noisy Action into an Output Action via the flow-matching ODE. This is the standard VLA stack Prism leaves untouched at inference [¶57].

[[part 4]]
CPR (Conditional Precision Regularization): the VLM's prefix hidden states, together with a prefix padding mask (1s and 0s), go through **mask-aware mean pooling** to form a pooled condition feature; a small Precision Predictor (Linear → SiLU → Linear → Sigmoid) turns it into a predicted demand \(\hat\rho\). The training signal is a precision regression loss between \(\hat\rho\) and the offline \(\rho\) from panel (a) — exactly Eq. (13), \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR},i}=(\hat\rho(c_i)-\rho_i)^2\) [¶72]. Importantly, the arrow goes only one way: \(\hat\rho\) never feeds back into sample weighting [¶73].

[[part 5]]
PSW (Precision-Scaled Weighting): the ground-truth action chunk gives its **Action RMS** (\(\sigma_{f,i}\) in Eq. (9) [¶47]), which together with **flow time** forms the flow-time visibility \(\Psi\) — the \((1-\tau)^p(1-e^{-\mathrm{SNR}/\tau_0})\) term of Eq. (11) [¶66]. That visibility is gated by the same offline \(\rho\) in the Precision Weighting node to produce \(w_i = 1+\gamma\rho_i\Psi_i\), which multiplies the flow-matching loss \(L_{FM}\) into a precision-weighted loss. The dashed "Combined Training Objective" arrow joins the CPR regression loss and this weighted loss into \(\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PSW}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{CPR}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR}}\) [¶74].

So the flow is: trajectories → PPS → \(\rho\) (once, offline) → {CPR target, PSW weight} → one combined loss; after training the CPR head and the \(\rho\) labels are discarded and the model runs as an ordinary VLA [¶57].

runs.question: apertus-unanswerable
runs.text:
**Short answer: the report gives neither a dollar cost nor a CO₂ figure.** It reports energy and GPU-hours only, and says the electricity is hydropower. Everything monetary or in tonnes below is my own arithmetic, not a claim from the paper.

## What the paper actually reports (Section 6.3, ¶370)

- Energy estimated as measured GPU-hours × an assumed 560 W per GH200 module (below the 660 W power cap on Alps): **≈225,000 GPU-hours** for the 8B continued-pretraining stages, **≈1.50 M** for the 70B, ≈2 M GPU-hours total including both long-context extensions, i.e. **≈1.1 GWh**.
- For scale: from-scratch Apertus 1.0 pretraining was **≈5 GWh** [¶370].
- Whole project duration: **9 M GPU-hours allocated**, an estimate of **≈5 GWh**, excluding idle time and other Swiss AI Initiative workloads [¶370].
- Per-phase throughput and segment counts (the basis of those GPU-hours) are in Table 40 [¶368]; runs used 256 nodes for the 8B and 512 for the 70B [¶361].
- Explicit caveat: the 1.1 GWh covers **logged production segments only** — it excludes post-training (SFT, RL, DPO, SDPO), evaluation, ablations and idle reservation time, so real consumption is higher [¶370].
- Carbon: the paper only states that "Alps draws on carbon-free hydropower, and CSCS cools the infrastructure with lake water in a closed cycle" [¶370]. No tonnes are given anywhere, and no cost in any currency.

## Back-of-envelope estimates (outside the paper)

Taking the paper's 1.1 GWh for continued pretraining and ~5 GWh for the whole campaign, with assumptions I am supplying:

| Basis | Continued pretraining (~1.1 GWh) | Whole campaign (~5 GWh) |
|---|---|---|
| Electricity only, at ~\$0.15–0.25/kWh | ~\$165k–275k | ~\$750k–1.25M |
| Grid lifecycle intensity, ~10–30 g CO₂-eq/kWh for hydro | ~11–33 t CO₂-eq | ~50–150 t CO₂-eq |

If you instead price the compute like a cloud rental (~\$3–6 per GH200-GPU-hour, which I cannot verify), 2 M logged GPU-hours is roughly \$6M–12M, and the full 9 M allocated GPU-hours would be roughly \$27M–54M — but that is hardware/ops amortisation, not something the report claims. Note the ordering: on this accounting the electricity line item is a fraction of a percent of the compute cost, so "cost to train" is dominated by machine amortisation, which the paper never prices.

Two cautions on the carbon number. First, the same ~5 GWh on a grid averaging ~400–500 g CO₂-eq/kWh would be ~2,000–2,500 t, so the alpine hydropower supply is what makes the figure small — the paper's "carbon-free" phrasing describes the supply mix, not a lifecycle assessment. Second, since post-training and evaluation are excluded from the 1.1 GWh and only the ~9 M-GPU-hour allocation window hints at them [¶370], both the energy and the derived cost and carbon figures are lower bounds on the true campaign footprint.

runs.question: dpo-derivation
runs.text:
## Setup: one substitution does most of the work

Write the per-response log-ratio as

\[
\rho_\theta(x,y)=\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)},
\qquad \hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\,\rho_\theta(x,y),
\]

so that Eq. (7) [¶33] is just

\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\,\mathbb E_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal D}\big[\log\sigma(h)\big],
\qquad h=\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_l).
\]

(Section A.4 [¶167]–[¶174] runs exactly this chain of differentiation.)

## The four steps

**1. Chain rule.** Differentiate $-\log\sigma(h)$ with respect to $\theta$:

\[
\nabla_\theta \mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\,\mathbb E\Big[\frac{\sigma'(h)}{\sigma(h)}\,\nabla_\theta h\Big]
\]

which is Eq. (22) [¶171]. Swapping gradient and expectation is fine since the expectation is over fixed data, and $\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)=\sum_t \log\pi_\theta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})$ is differentiable in $\theta$ (the discrete sampling of RLHF never enters here — that's what makes DPO a supervised-style loss).

**2. Use the sigmoid identities** [¶172]. With $\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\big(1-\sigma(z)\big)$, the prefactor simplifies:

\[
\frac{\sigma'(h)}{\sigma(h)}=1-\sigma(h)=\sigma(-h)=\sigma\!\left(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\right).
\]

So the prefactor is *"how wrongly the implicit reward ranks the pair"*, and it lands in $(0,1)$: $\approx 1$ if the model still rates $y_l$ above $y_w$, $\approx 0$ once the pair is separated by a comfortable margin.

**3. Differentiate the inside.** $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is frozen and does not depend on $\theta$, so only $\log\pi_\theta$ survives:

\[
\nabla_\theta h=\beta\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)-\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)\big].
\]

**4. Combine** (the $-$ from step 2 times the $\beta$ from step 3):

\[
\nabla_\theta \mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\beta\,\mathbb E_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\underbrace{\sigma\!\left(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\right)}_{\text{weight: big when the pair is mis-ranked}}\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)-\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)\big]\Big],
\]

which is the displayed gradient in Section 4 [¶37] and its interpretation in [¶38]: push up the log-probability of $y_w$, push down $y_l$, with per-example weight scaled by $\beta$. The same structure shows up in the reference implementation [¶200]: `losses = -logsigmoid(beta * (pi_logratios - ref_logratios))`, where the two log-ratios are just $\hat r_\theta/\beta$ for $y_w$ and $y_l$.

## Why the weight matters

Drop $\sigma(\cdot)$ (i.e. set the weight to 1) and you get "maximize $\log p(y_w\mid x)$, minimize $\log p(y_l\mid x)$" — the Unlikelihood baseline [¶62][¶218]. The paper reports that this unconstrained likelihood minimization degenerates into repetitions such as endless "when" tokens on TL;DR (Table 3 [¶219][¶220]), which is the empirical justification for the term that steps 1–2 produce.

## One caution about the appendix's signs

Taken literally, Eq. (21) [¶169] and the final line [¶173] write the sigmoid argument with $y_l$ and $y_w$ in the opposite order from Eq. (7) — i.e. $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(y_w)-\hat r_\theta(y_l))$ rather than $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(y_l)-\hat r_\theta(y_w))$. The gradient of Eq. (7) as printed in the main text [¶37] is the version above with $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$; it is also the only one consistent with the stated intuition that the weight grows "when the reward estimate is wrong" [¶37][¶38]. So treat that as a notational slip in Appendix A.4 rather than a different result.

runs.question: dpo-detail
runs.text:
**TL;DR summarization DPO run (Appendix B, ¶201 + Section 6.2, ¶67):**

| Hyperparameter | Value |
|---|---|
| \(\beta\) (KL penalty) | **0.5** (the paper's default is 0.1; TL;DR is the stated exception) |
| Optimizer | **RMSprop** |
| Learning rate | **1e-6**, linearly warmed up from 0 to 1e-6 over **150 steps** |
| Batch size | **64** |

So the sentence in Appendix B that pins this down is: "Unless noted otherwise, we use a \(\beta = 0.1\), batch size of 64 and the RMSprop optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-6 by default. We linearly warmup the learning rate from 0 to 1e-6 over 150 steps. For TL;DR summarization, we use \(\beta = 0.5\), while rest of the parameters remain the same." [¶201]

Other setup details you'd need for that run:

- **Reference / initial policy:** \(\pi_{\text{ref}} = \pi^{\mathrm{SFT}}\), the GPT-J TL;DR SFT model from CarperAI (`CarperAI/openai_summarize_tldr_sft`); DPO, PPO and Preferred-FT all fine-tune this same SFT model. [¶67][¶72] Satisfies the paper's rule of using the SFT model as reference when it is available [¶38].
- **Data:** Reddit TL;DR summarization dataset [43] with the human preference labels from Stiennon et al. [¶58]; a preference pair is \((x, y_w, y_l)\) fed to the loss in Eq. (7) [¶33].
- **Loss implementation:** Appendix B gives the code — sequence-level log-probs for policy and reference, `losses = -logsigmoid(beta * ((pi_yw - pi_yl) - (ref_yw - ref_yl)))`, with `rewards = beta * (pi_logps - ref_logps).detach()` logged as the implicit reward \(\hat r_\theta\). [¶200]
- **Evaluation:** win rates vs. reference test summaries, sampled at temperatures 0.0–1.0 with GPT-4 as judge (the "concise" GPT-4 (C) prompt); DPO reached ~61% at temp 0.0, and the OOD CNN/DailyMail run used temps 0 and 0.25. [¶67][¶70][¶74][¶211]

Two caveats for reproducing exactly:

1. The paper does **not** report the number of epochs/gradient steps, weight decay, sequence-length limits, or whether full fine-tuning vs. parameter-efficient tuning was used for the TL;DR run — only Appendix C.1 gives such detail, and that is for the IMDb sentiment experiment. [¶205] So those choices you'd have to infer or sweep.
2. \(\beta=0.5\) is the only \(\beta\) used for TL;DR; the sweep \(\beta \in \{0.05, 0.1, 1, 5\}\) belongs to the controlled sentiment experiment [¶64]. The authors also note they "did not meaningfully tune DPO's \(\beta\)" for summarization, so 0.5 is closer to a default than an optimized value [¶67].

runs.question: dpo-figure
runs.text:
**Short answer: no — the plot shows Best of 128 above the 50% line at every temperature too.** The caption's claim is true only with the qualifier the main text adds: DPO is the only *computationally efficient* method to beat the chosen responses ([¶68]).

## What the left panel plots

[[part 1]]

The left panel shows GPT-4 win rate against the preferred ("chosen") completion in the Anthropic-HH test set, as a function of sampling temperature, for four methods: DPO, Best of 128, Preferred-FT, and the base Pythia-2.8B. The dashed line at 0.5 is parity — a method above it produces responses GPT-4 prefers over the human-labelled best responses in the dataset; below it, worse. Three temperatures are plotted (≈0.25, a mid value, and 1.0), with error bars on each point [¶60].

[[part 2]]

**At the lowest temperature (0.25) the two methods are far apart, and Best of 128 wins.** Best of 128 sits at roughly 0.54 (error bar ≈0.51–0.58), i.e. above parity, while DPO is at roughly 0.37–0.39 (error bar ≈0.33–0.42), clearly *below* parity. The error bars do not overlap, so at this temperature DPO is not merely worse than Best of 128 — it is worse than the dataset's own preferred responses. This alone contradicts a literal reading of "DPO is the only method that improves over chosen summaries."

[[part 3]]

**At the mid and high temperatures the two are effectively tied, with DPO edging ahead.** At the middle temperature both curves land at ≈0.60 and their error bars overlap almost completely. At temperature 1.0, DPO is nominally higher (≈0.63, bar ≈0.61–0.66) than Best of 128 (≈0.60, bar ≈0.59–0.62), but the bars still overlap, so the gap is not clearly resolvable from the plot. The reliable reading is "matches or slightly exceeds," which is how the text puts it: DPO "provides similar or better performance to the computationally demanding Best of 128 baseline" [¶68].

For completeness, the two supervised baselines never cross 0.5: Preferred-FT peaks near 0.42 at the mid temperature and falls back to ≈0.37, and Pythia-2.8B stays between ≈0.16 and ≈0.25 [¶60].

## Why the caption is misleading, and what the paper actually claims

The caption drops the word that does the work. Section 6.2 states the claim as: "DPO is the only **computationally efficient** method that improves over the preferred completions in the Anthropic HH dataset" [¶68]. Best of 128 is above parity in the plot precisely because it draws 128 samples per prompt at *test* time and returns the highest-reward one, which the paper describes as "computationally impractical even for moderate N" [¶62] and notes plateaus around 64–128 samples [¶226]. Best of 128 is used as a stand-in for PPO-level quality because the authors could not get their PPO baseline to beat the base model on this task [¶68]. So the honest summary of the left panel is: at matched, practical cost, DPO is the only method above 0.5 — but only at temperatures around 0.7 and above, and its advantage over Best of 128 is within the error bars.

[[part 4]]

The right panel is a different comparison — DPO against itself over training. Win rate versus fine-tuning step at temperatures 1.0 and 0.7 starts below parity (≈0.33–0.40), crosses 0.5 by roughly step 300, then fluctuates between about 0.51 and 0.64 with no sustained further gain, and a mild downward drift at the end of training. This supports the text's claim that "DPO converges to its best performance relatively quickly" [¶68]; the authors flag the late decline as a possible instance of reward over-optimization, left open for future work [¶78].

One caution: all numbers above are read off the plot by eye, since the paper gives no table of the dialogue win rates.

runs.question: dpo-visual
runs.text:
**One DPO step, in words** (then the diagram below):

**1. Where the pair comes from.** You first have an offline preference dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(x^{(i)}, y_w^{(i)}, y_l^{(i)})\}$ built by sampling two completions from the reference policy for each prompt $x$ and having humans pick the better one, $y_w \succ y_l \mid x$ [¶18][¶38]. If no SFT model is available, $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is made by likelihood-training on the chosen completions only [¶38].

**2. Two forward passes, no sampling.** For one pair, the trainable policy $\pi_\theta$ and a *frozen* reference $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ each score both responses (sequence log-probs). This is the whole compute cost of a step — no generation, no reward model, no value function [¶10][¶55], and the PyTorch implementation is only a few lines [¶200].

**3. Form the implicit reward.** From each response's log-ratio against the reference,
$\hat r_\theta(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)}$ — this is exactly the reparameterization in Eq. (5), and it is what "your language model is secretly a reward model" means [¶29][¶38][¶42].

**4. Take the difference.** The quantity that matters is the margin $\hat r_\theta(x,y_w) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_l)$. The intractable partition function $Z(x)$ drops out because the Bradley–Terry model only depends on reward *differences* for the same prompt [¶30][¶31] (Eq. 6).

**5. Binary cross-entropy loss.** $\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}\right)$ (Eq. 7) [¶33] — the same likelihood loss used to fit an explicit reward model (Eq. 2), but applied to the policy directly.

**6. What the update does.** The gradient raises $\log \pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)$ and lowers $\log \pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)$, weighted by $\sigma\!\left(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\right)$, i.e. examples the implicit reward currently ranks *wrongly* get more weight; dropping this weight degenerates the model [¶37][¶38]. Only $\pi_\theta$ is updated; $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ stays fixed.

Typical single-step hyperparameters: $\beta = 0.1$ (0.5 for TL;DR), batch 64, RMSprop at LR 1e-6 with a 150-step warmup [¶201].

input.title: One DPO training step: from a preference pair to the loss
input.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    data["Offline preference set D: prompt x, chosen y_w, rejected y_l"] --> pair["Take one pair (x, y_w, y_l)"]
    pair --> pol["Policy pi_theta (trainable, init from SFT)"]
    pair --> ref["Reference pi_ref (frozen, no gradients)"]
    pol --> plog["log pi_theta(y_w|x), log pi_theta(y_l|x)"]
    ref --> rlog["log pi_ref(y_w|x), log pi_ref(y_l|x)"]
    plog --> rhat["Implicit reward r_hat(x,y) = beta * log(pi_theta / pi_ref)"]
    rlog --> rhat
    rhat --> marg["Margin: r_hat(x,y_w) minus r_hat(x,y_l); Z(x) cancels"]
    marg --> loss["Loss = -log sigmoid(beta * (policy logratio - ref logratio))"]
    loss --> upd["Backprop, update pi_theta only"]
    upd --> grad["Weight sigma(r_hat(y_l) - r_hat(y_w)) boosts mis-ranked pairs"]

runs.question: mamba-equation
runs.text:
## The short version

Equation (4) is the **discretization step**: it turns the *continuous-time* parameters of an SSM, $(\Delta, \boldsymbol{A}, \boldsymbol{B})$, into the *discrete-time* parameters $(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})$ that actually appear in the recurrence the model runs on sampled data. It is one specific choice of discretization rule — the **zero-order hold (ZOH)** — out of several possible ones [¶25][¶26].

$$\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = \exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}), \qquad \overline{\boldsymbol{B}} = (\Delta \boldsymbol{A})^{-1}\left(\exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A}) - \boldsymbol{I}\right)\cdot \Delta \boldsymbol{B} \tag{4}$$

## Where it sits in the pipeline

The SSM is defined in two stages [¶23][¶24]:

1. Continuous system: $h'(t) = \boldsymbol{A}h(t) + \boldsymbol{B}x(t)$, $y(t) = \boldsymbol{C}h(t)$ — Eq. (1).
2. Discrete recurrence: $h_t = \overline{\boldsymbol{A}}h_{t-1} + \overline{\boldsymbol{B}}x_t$, $y_t = \boldsymbol{C}h_t$ — Eq. (2).

Equation (4) is exactly the map from (1) to (2): $f_{\boldsymbol{A}}(\Delta,\boldsymbol{A})$ and $f_{\boldsymbol{B}}(\Delta,\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{B})$ [¶25]. Mechanically, it is "the first step of the computation graph in the forward pass of an SSM" [¶27]. Note that $\boldsymbol{C}$ is untouched — it already acts on the discrete state.

## What each symbol means

| Symbol | Meaning | Shape (diagonal SSM) |
|---|---|---|
| $x(t)$, $x_t$ | Input, continuous signal vs. sampled sequence | scalar per channel |
| $h(t) \in \mathbb{R}^N$ | Implicit latent state that summarizes history | $N$ |
| $\boldsymbol{A}$ | Continuous-time **state transition / decay matrix**: how the state evolves on its own between inputs | $N \times N$, taken diagonal, so $N$ numbers [¶33][¶34] |
| $\boldsymbol{B}$ | Continuous-time **input projection**: how much the input is injected into the state | $N \times 1$ [¶34] |
| $\Delta$ | The **discretization step size** — a timescale / sampling period. It is the only quantity that knows "how much time passes between two tokens" | scalar (per position) |
| $\exp(\cdot)$ | Matrix exponential (elementwise here, since $\boldsymbol{A}$ is diagonal) | — |
| $\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ | **Discrete decay**: multiply by this to advance the state one step | $N$ numbers |
| $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}$ | **Discrete input weight**: how much of $x_t$ enters $h_t$ | $N$ numbers |

## Where the two formulas come from

Solve the ODE $h'(t) = \boldsymbol{A}h(t) + \boldsymbol{B}x(t)$ exactly over one interval of length $\Delta$.

- **Homogeneous part.** With no input, $h(t+\Delta) = e^{\Delta \boldsymbol{A}} h(t)$, which is precisely $\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = \exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A})$. Since $\boldsymbol{A}$ is diagonal and negative-real, each entry is a decay factor in $(0,1)$ — the state's memory.
- **Forced part.** "Zero-order hold" means assume $x(t)$ is *held constant* across the step (you only have samples, so the input is piecewise-constant). Integrating the input contribution gives $\int_0^{\Delta} e^{\tau \boldsymbol{A}} d\tau\;\boldsymbol{B} x_t$, and that integral evaluates to $(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})^{-1}(e^{\Delta\boldsymbol{A}} - \boldsymbol{I})\Delta\boldsymbol{B}$ — exactly $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}$.

So $\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}$ answers "how much of the old state survives one step," and $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}$ answers "how much of this step's input gets accumulated into the state."

**Scalar/diagonal case** (each mode $n$ separately, writing $a$ and $b$):
$$\bar{a} = e^{\Delta a}, \qquad \bar{b} = \frac{e^{\Delta a}-1}{a}\, b .$$

Two useful sanity checks from the paper's own Appendix C proof [¶362]: with $\boldsymbol{A}=-1, \boldsymbol{B}=1$, you get $\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = \sigma(-\text{Linear}(x_t)) = 1-g_t$ and $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}} = 1-\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} = g_t$, which collapses Eq. (4) into the gated recurrence of Theorem 1, $h_t = (1-g_t)h_{t-1} + g_t x_t$ [¶84][¶85]. That is the sense in which $\Delta$ "plays a generalized role of the RNN gating mechanism" [¶83].

## Why this matters for Mamba specifically

- **$\Delta$ is the lever of selection.** Mamba makes $\Delta$ (and $\boldsymbol{B}, \boldsymbol{C}$) functions of the input [¶55][¶56], so $\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}_t, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_t$ vary with $t$ — the model becomes time-varying, loses the convolution equivalence, and needs the selective scan [¶30][¶32][¶68].
- **Making $\boldsymbol{A}$ selective is redundant.** $\boldsymbol{A}$ affects the model *only* through (4), via $\exp(\Delta \boldsymbol{A})$; selectivity in $\Delta$ already induces selectivity in $(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})$ [¶94].
- **Interpretation of $\Delta$**, via (4): $\Delta \to \infty$ gives $\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} \to 0$ (forget state, take in the current input); $\Delta \to 0$ gives $\overline{\boldsymbol{A}} \to \boldsymbol{I}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}} \to 0$ (ignore this input, keep the state) [¶93][¶91].

## Two caveats

1. Some SSM variants skip (4) entirely and parameterize $(\overline{\boldsymbol{A}}, \overline{\boldsymbol{B}})$ directly, which can be easier to reason about [¶27].
2. *(Outside the paper, not stated in it)*: the factor $(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})^{-1}(\exp(\Delta\boldsymbol{A})-\boldsymbol{I})$ is a matrix $(e^z - 1)/z$-type function with a *removable* singularity at $z = 0$, so implementations evaluate it by its Taylor series for small $\Delta a$ rather than forming a literal inverse. The paper does not discuss this numerical detail.

runs.question: mamba-figure
runs.text:
**Short answer:** Mamba 1.4B peaks at **1814 tokens/s** at batch size 128 (the largest batch shown). The Transformer 1.3B never gets that far — its best is **443 tokens/s** at batch 32, after which it is marked **OOM** at batches 64 and 128. That peak-to-peak ratio is ≈ **4.1×**, which is what the caption's "5×" rounds up from; the body text states the range more carefully as "4–5× higher inference throughput" ([¶162]).

**Reading the right panel in detail** ([¶163], protocol in Appendix E.5 [¶495][¶496] — A100 80GB, prompt length 2048, 128 generated tokens, standard HuggingFace Transformer implementation):

- Batch 1 → 16: Mamba 1.4B roughly doubles with batch each time (140 → 247 → 441 → 744 → 1089), and the Transformer 1.3B does the same but at about 55–60% of Mamba's value (79 → 132 → 199 → 265 → 323). Ratio in this regime: ~1.8× → 3.4×.
- Batch 32: Mamba 1.4B 1445 vs Transformer 1.3B 443 (~3.3×) — the Transformer is close to saturating its memory.
- Batches 64 and 128: the Transformer 1.3B bars are replaced by "OOM" labels; Mamba 1.4B keeps climbing to 1668 and 1814. This is the actual source of the headline gap — Mamba's peak is reachable *only because* the Transformer cannot run at those batch sizes.
- The 6.9B pair tells the same story with more headroom for Mamba: Mamba 6.9B goes 58 → 515 across batches 1 → 128, while Transformer 6.7B reaches only 123 at batch 16 and OOMs from batch 32 on. [¶162] draws the corollary that "a Mamba-6.9B (untrained) would have higher inference throughput than a 5× smaller Transformer-1.3B" (515 vs 443) — note this is a *different* 5×, about model size, not throughput.

**Why the gap exists, per the paper:** Mamba is fully recurrent, so autoregressive generation costs constant time per step with no KV cache to store, which lets it use much larger batches on the same GPU ([¶13][¶162]). Attention-based decoding must keep the whole context cached, giving linear-time inference and a memory ceiling that hits at batch 32–64 here.

**One caveat worth keeping in mind:** the paper does not spell out the arithmetic behind "5×" ([¶4][¶17][¶163]); the only explicit range is "4–5×" in Section 4.5 ([¶162]). Also, the Transformer baseline is the stock HuggingFace implementation rather than the fused/FlashAttention path used elsewhere in the paper ([¶495]), so part of the measured ratio reflects implementation maturity, not architecture alone.

runs.question: muon-critical
runs.text:
**Short answer: no to both.** Theorem 3 is an approximate‑criticality result, not a global‑optimality result, and the paper never claims the rate carries over to the capped variant of Appendix E.2.1.

## What Theorem 3 actually gives

The setting is *nonconvex*: Assumptions 1–3 only give \(L\)-smoothness, lower boundedness, and an unbiased gradient oracle with bounded variance \(\sigma^2\) ([¶24]–[¶29]). There is no convexity, no PL/Łojasiewicz condition, and nothing else that could support a global-minimum claim.

The conclusion ([¶64]) is

\[ \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\Big[\|P^{\top}\nabla F(W_{t})\|_{*}+\|Q\nabla F(W_{t})\|_{F}\Big]\le O(T^{-1/4}), \]

i.e. a Cesàro-averaged first-order stationarity statement. So:

- It bounds a **stationarity measure**, not \(F(W_t)-F_*\). By Remark 5 ([¶68]) and the final display of the proof ([¶300]) this mixed measure dominates \(\|\nabla F(W_t)\|_F\), so the average full-gradient norm also decays at \(T^{-1/4}\) — that is the strongest notion available here, and it says "you find a near-stationary iterate," not "you found the minimum."
- It is an **average over iterates**: individual iterates (including the last one) are not controlled.
- It holds **for any fixed orthonormal basis \(P\)**, including a noise-dominated one ([¶63]). That generality is the point: the residual correction, not the subspace quality, buys convergence.
- The stated rate requires the prescribed scalings \(\beta=\Theta(T^{-1/2})\), \(\eta=\Theta(T^{-3/4})\), \(\gamma=\Theta(T^{1/4})\) with \(L\eta\gamma\le 1\) ([¶63]), and the constant grows with \(r\), \(\sigma^2\) and \(\Delta\) ([¶298]).
- It is written for a **single matrix parameter** \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\); the paper does not restate it for the whole network's summed loss.

Multi-stage Theorem 4 is the same type of statement, and additionally assumes equal stage lengths with \(K=T\), \(N=KT\) ([¶75][¶315]).

## Why the rate does not transfer automatically to the capped implementation

The practical variant is introduced empirically — "applies a residual cap to improve training stability" ([¶81], [¶442]) — and no theorem is attached to it. Concrete deviations from Algorithms 3–4:

- **Time-varying, data-dependent residual weight.** The cap replaces the constant \(\gamma\) by \(\widehat\gamma_{k,t}=\min\{\gamma,\rho\sqrt{\|P_kZ_{k,t}\|_F^2/\max\{\|R_{k,t}\|_F^2,\epsilon\}}\}\) ([¶446]), which enforces \(\|\widehat\gamma_{k,t}R_{k,t}\|_F\le\rho\|P_kZ_{k,t}\|_F\). The proofs use \(\gamma\) as a fixed scalar throughout (the descent term \(\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\bar S\) and the noise term \(L\eta\gamma^2\sigma^2/2\) in Lemma 5, [¶279]; the condition \(L\eta\gamma\le1\)). Worse, the cap attenuates the residual exactly when the projected Muon direction is small — precisely the regime where residual descent matters — so nothing in the bound on \(\bar R\) survives unchanged.
- **Two extra terms not in the algorithm.** The practical update carries a shape-dependent factor \(0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\) and a weight-decay term \(-\eta\lambda W_{k,t}\) ([¶444][¶447]), both inherited from Liu et al. (2025) rather than analyzed. Weight decay contributes \(\langle \nabla F(W),\lambda W\rangle\), which is not controlled under Assumptions 1–3 (no iterate boundedness is assumed).
- **Approximate msign.** \( \operatorname{msign} \) is computed with 5 Newton–Schulz iterations ([¶459]). The proof uses the exact identities \(\langle X,\operatorname{msign}(X)\rangle=\|X\|_*\) and \(\|\operatorname{msign}(X)\|_2\le1\) ([¶253], Lemmas 1–2, [¶259]–[¶266]); truncating them turns the argument into an unquantified approximation-error statement.
- **Momentum form differs.** Experiments use Nesterov momentum with coefficient \(1-\beta=0.95\) ([¶459]); Algorithms 3–4 use the plain EMA \(M_t=(1-\beta)M_{t-1}+\beta P^{\top}G_t\) ([¶60]).
- **Mixed optimizer.** 1-D and embedding parameters are trained with AdamW ([¶459]), so a subset of parameters is never covered by PMRC at all.
- **Hyperparameters are not in the theoretical regime.** \(\gamma=8192\)–\(16384\) and \(\mathrm{lr}=2\times10^{-3}\)–\(5\times10^{-3}\) (Table 7, [¶456]) with refresh interval 100 ([¶84]), versus \(\gamma=\Theta(N^{1/4})\), \(\eta=\Theta(N^{-3/4})\) ([¶75]).

One thing that *is* covered: the warm-started QR basis refresh \(P=\mathrm{QR}(G f_{\mathrm{RN}}((P^{\mathrm{prev}})^{\top}G)^{\top})\) ([¶449]) returns an orthonormal basis chosen from the history before the stage, which is exactly Assumption 4 ([¶31]). Theorem 4 explicitly allows such arbitrary adaptive bases (cf. Remark 3 for SMRC, [¶54]). So the approximate SVD is not what breaks the guarantee — the cap, weight decay, truncated msign and Nesterov are.

**Reading the two together:** Theorem 3/4 justify the *design principle* (keep momentum in the subspace, add the orthogonal residual back), and Tables 1–2 plus Figures 4–5 ([¶473][¶475]) show the capped implementation works in practice. The formal guarantee for the implementation as run is a gap the paper leaves open, not something Theorem 3 supplies.

runs.question: muon-detail
runs.text:
Appendix E.2.1 keeps the Algorithm 4 skeleton but adds two practical modifications, each with its own settings and supporting numbers.

## 1. A residual cap on the orthogonal-correction term

**Why.** With a single global coefficient \(\gamma\), the residual and projected directions cannot stay aligned across parameter blocks and steps: early in training the initial subspace can leave a large fraction of the gradient in the orthogonal complement, so that \(\gamma\lVert (I-P_kP_k^{\top})G_{k,t}\rVert_F\) greatly exceeds \(\lVert P_k Z_{k,t}\rVert_F\), and the authors observed this coincides with pronounced loss fluctuations [¶442].

**What.** With \(R_{k,t}=(I-P_kP_k^{\top})G_{k,t}\), the update becomes [¶444][¶446]

\[ W_{k,t+1}=W_{k,t}-0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\,\eta\big(P_kZ_{k,t}+\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}R_{k,t}\big)-\eta\lambda W_{k,t}, \]
\[ \widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}=\min\Big\{\gamma,\ \rho\sqrt{\tfrac{\lVert P_kZ_{k,t}\rVert_F^2}{\max\{\lVert R_{k,t}\rVert_F^2,\epsilon\}}}\Big\}, \]

so the correction is clipped to satisfy \(\lVert\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}R_{k,t}\rVert_F\le \rho\lVert P_kZ_{k,t}\rVert_F\), while the full \(\gamma\) is kept whenever the residual is already below that threshold [¶442][¶477]. The shape-dependent factor \(0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}}\) and the weight decay \(\lambda\) are the standard Muon practicalities, inherited from Liu et al. (2025) [¶447].

**Settings and evidence.** \(\rho=4\) and \(\epsilon=10^{-30}\) [¶447]. In the ablations (LLaMA-150M, 9900 steps, sequence length 512, global batch 512, refresh every 100 steps, \(r=256\), \(\gamma=8192\)), the capped run with \(\rho=4\) is stable whereas the uncapped run becomes unstable during early training (Figure 5) [¶471][¶473][¶475]. The \(\gamma\) values actually used in pretraining are 8192 (60M) and 16384 (150M/350M/1.3B) [¶456]; for SFT, \(\gamma\) is grid-searched over \(\{2000,4000,8000,16000\}\) with the cap ratio fixed at 4 [¶465].

## 2. A cheap warm-started basis refresh replacing exact SVD

**Why.** Periodic exact SVDs (as in GaLore) add time overhead whenever the basis is refreshed, especially for high-dimensional matrices [¶448].

**What.** Given the gradient matrix \(G\) and the previous basis \(P^{\mathrm{prev}}\), the new basis is computed as [¶449][¶450]

\[ P=\operatorname{QR}\!\left(G\,f_{\mathrm{RN}}\!\left((P^{\mathrm{prev}})^{\top}G\right)^{\top}\right), \]

where \(f_{\mathrm{RN}}\) normalizes rows and QR returns an orthonormal basis; this is a warm-started subspace approximation adapted from ARO (Gong et al., 2026), the singular values are estimated from the row norms of \(P^{\top}G\), and the QR itself is computed with shifted Cholesky QR, SCQR (Fukaya et al., 2020) [¶448][¶450].

**Timing evidence (Table 3).** Per-matrix projector latency on LLaMA-350M shapes, one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU [¶451][¶452]:

| Matrix shape | Exact SVD | Ours | Approx. speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 × 1024 | 58.01 ms | 3.21 ms | ~18× |
| 2736 × 1024 | 57.75 ms | 2.98 ms | ~19× |
| 1024 × 2736 | 57.36 ms | 2.98 ms | ~19× |

The paper summarizes this as roughly 3 ms versus nearly 58 ms per refresh [¶452].

One caveat worth noting: both changes are implementation-level, and the convergence theorems (Theorems 3 and 4) are stated for the uncapped update with \(\gamma=\Theta(T^{1/4})\) and an exact orthonormal basis [¶64][¶71][¶75]; the cap means the effective residual weight is an upper bound rather than the value used in the analysis [¶473].

runs.question: prism-false_premise
runs.text:
**Short answer: CPR is the *smallest* contributor — about +0.10 of the +0.60 total on drive connector insertion (0.35 → 0.45).** And the premise needs correcting: CPR never "signals" the action expert at test time.

## What CPR is actually doing

CPR adds one auxiliary loss: an MLP head predicts the offline precision score \(\rho_i\) from the mask-pooled VLM condition representation \(h_{c_i}\), i.e. \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPR},i}=(\hat\rho(c_i)-\rho_i)^2\) (Eq. 13, [¶72]). Its only lasting effect is that the *representation itself* gets shaped to encode precision demand. The prediction head and the auxiliary labels are **discarded after training**, and the backbone and its standard ODE solver are unchanged at inference [¶57][¶11][¶75]. So at test time the action expert sees nothing but ordinary VLM conditioning tokens — no \(\hat\rho\), no extra module.

## Where the insertion gain actually comes from

Table 4 is a left-to-right cumulative ablation on drive insertion [¶95]:

| Configuration | Success | Increment | Attempts |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\pi_{0.5}\) base | 0.35 | — | 4.1 |
| + CPR | 0.45 | **+0.10** | 3.5 |
| + \(\rho\) (precision weight) | 0.70 | +0.25 | 2.7 |
| + \(\tau\) (clean-end emphasis) | 0.85 | +0.15 | 2.4 |
| + SNR gate (full Prism) | 0.95 | +0.10 | 2.1 |

CPR supplies roughly one-sixth of the total gain; the three PSW components together supply the other five-sixths (+0.50). The mechanism analysis is consistent with this: CPR alone "lowers overall residuals but worsens two lower-demand bins," so recognizing precision demand by itself does not ensure balanced action learning; adding PSW improves every bin (Figure 5(b), [¶101]).

Two caveats on reading those numbers:
- Because the rows are cumulative, +0.10 is CPR's **standalone** contribution. The paper does not report a "PSW without CPR" row, so CPR's marginal contribution inside the full model cannot be isolated from what is shown.
- CPR does appear to matter more than its standalone step suggests in one respect: it learns demand from vision-language features, not proprioception. Removing VLM state inputs drops the baseline from 0.35 to 0.30 while Prism stays at 0.95, and on \(\pi_0\) (state fed to the action expert instead) Prism still lifts 0.25 → 0.80 (Table 5, [¶96][¶103]).

The full 0.35 → 0.95 figure is the end-to-end real-robot result for \(\pi_{0.5}\) + Prism on drive insertion (Table 3, [¶91]).

input.title: Where the drive-insertion gain comes from (CPR vs PSW)
input.html:
Cumulative ablation, drive connector insertion (Table 4). Bars = end-to-end success; tags = increment over the row above. Amber = CPR alone.

No test-time signal. The CPR head and the offline labels are dropped after training; architecture and ODE solver are unchanged. CPR only shapes the pooled VLM condition feature via \((\hat\rho(c_i)-\rho_i)^2\).

runs.question: prism-figure_layout
runs.text:
Figure 3 is Prism's whole pipeline in one picture, and the key to reading it is that **one number — the offline precision demand ρ — is computed once on the left and then used twice at the bottom**. The left column is data preparation that happens before training; the bottom two dashed boxes are the two training objectives that both consume that number; the top middle/right is the untouched VLA backbone (VLM + flow-matching action expert) that they plug into. Nothing in the figure adds a module at inference time — the auxiliary labels and the prediction head are discarded after training [¶57].

[[part 1]]
**Part 1 — PPS: turning a demonstration into a precision label.** The three photos at the top are the stages of the real drive-insertion task (cable pickup → bimanual handover → connector insertion) along the time axis. Under them, "trajectory-derived signals" shows the three raw cues PPS reads: joint motion, end-effector motion, and gripper engagement. Joint and end-effector displacement are combined as \(s_i=\alpha_q\Delta q_i+\alpha_e\Delta e_i\) and converted to *relative slowness* by percentile rank over active frames, \(\operatorname{slow}_i=1-\operatorname{rank}_{\text{episode}}(s_i)\); the gripper trace supplies *motion validity*, an engagement factor \(g_i^{\text{eng}}\) and a gate \(t_i\) that suppresses rapid closing and isolated gripper motion [¶61]. The product is the frame-level demand \(\rho_i=g_i^{\text{eng}}\operatorname{slow}_i t_i\) [¶62]. So the logic is: slow, engaged, deliberately-held motion ⇒ precision is being demanded.

[[part 2]]
**Part 2 — the offline demand trace.** Two rows of frames from an episode, each with a colored strip beneath it and a shared Low (teal) → High (red) colorbar. This is \(\rho\) over time: it stays low through approach/handover and rises across the alignment-and-insertion interval. Two details matter for how it is used later: fixed neutral values are applied to disengaged and near-pause frames, then the trace is smoothed and clipped to \([0,1]\) [¶63], and each anchor frame contributes exactly one label to its action chunk — PSW does not average or maximize future \(\rho\) inside a chunk [¶63]. This whole column runs before optimization and is frozen [¶57].

[[part 3]]
**Part 3 — the condition stream of the backbone.** Three camera views go through a vision encoder, and their output tokens (pink) are concatenated with language-instruction tokens (blue, "Insert the cable into the motor drive.") and discretized-state tokens (green, `[STATE] 79 66 212 …`). These form the VLM prefix, whose hidden states come out at the bottom in matching colors. This is the quantity CPR operates on: the mask-pooled prefix features \(h_{c_i}\) [¶71].

[[part 4]]
**Part 4 — the action stream.** At the top right, the noisy action (dashed, jagged line) is the flow-time interpolation \(x_\tau=(1-\tau)z^*+\tau\epsilon\) with target velocity \(u_\tau=\epsilon-z^*\), integrated from \(\tau=1\) (noise) to \(\tau=0\) (clean) [¶29][¶30]. It enters the Action Expert, which predicts the velocity \(v_\theta\); the plain flow-matching loss is \(L_{FM}\). PSW attaches exactly here — as a scalar multiplier on that loss — which is why the architecture and the ODE solver are unchanged [¶57][¶68].

[[part 5]]
**Part 5 — CPR: making precision demand readable from the condition.** Prefix hidden states plus the prefix padding mask feed a *mask-aware mean pooling* block (padding positions carry mask 0 and are excluded), giving one pooled condition feature. A small MLP head — Linear → SiLU → Linear → Sigmoid — outputs the predicted demand \(\hat\rho\), trained against the offline \(\rho\) with a precision regression loss \((\hat\rho(c_i)-\rho_i)^2\) [¶72]. The two thin strips visualize prediction versus target tracking each other. Crucially, \(\hat\rho\) is never fed back into weighting: PSW keeps using the offline \(\rho_i\) [¶73].

[[part 6]]
**Part 6 — PSW: spending extra supervision where it counts.** Three inputs combine. The GT action chunk gives its RMS scale \(\sigma_{f,i}\), which with flow time \(\tau_i\) yields \(\operatorname{SNR}_i=(1-\tau_i)^2\sigma_{f,i}^2/(\tau_i^2+\varepsilon)\) [¶47]; that becomes *flow-time visibility* \(\Psi_i=(1-\tau_i)^{p}\bigl(1-e^{-\operatorname{SNR}_i/\tau_0}\bigr)\), a clean-end emphasis multiplied by a saturating "is the signal visible yet?" gate [¶66]; and the offline \(\rho\) enters *precision weighting*, \(w_i=1+\gamma\rho_i\Psi_i\in[1,1+\gamma]\). That weight multiplies the chunk's \(L_{FM}\) (the ⊗ node) to give the precision-weighted loss, which joins CPR's regression loss in the Combined Training Objective \(\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{PSW}}+\lambda_{\text{CPR}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CPR}}\) [¶68][¶74]. Since \(w_i\ge 1\), PSW only adds supervision — it never withdraws it from routine samples [¶67].

**How the pieces connect, in one line:** PPS measures demand from the demonstration (Parts 1–2) → CPR teaches the VLM condition to recognize that demand from vision/language/state alone (Part 5) → PSW spends extra flow-matching gradient on high-demand samples, but only once their action signal is actually visible in the noise (Part 6) → both losses sum into one training objective, and everything auxiliary is dropped at inference. On drive insertion the parts contribute cumulatively: 0.35 baseline → 0.45 with CPR → 0.70 with precision weighting → 0.85 with clean-end emphasis → 0.95 with SNR gating [¶95][¶97].

runs.question: apertus-unanswerable
runs.text:
**The report does not give a dollar cost or a carbon footprint in tonnes of CO₂.** It reports GPU-hours and estimated electricity use, which provide a basis for rough estimates—but not verified cost or emissions totals. [¶370]

Section 6.3 gives two scopes:

| Scope | GPU-hours | Estimated electricity |
|---|---:|---:|
| Logged production continued pretraining and long-context extension, both models | ~2 million | ~1.1 GWh |
| Whole-project allocation | ~9 million | ~5 GWh |

The production figure excludes post-training, evaluations, ablations, and idle reservation time; the broader project estimate also excludes idle time. [¶370]

**Illustrative dollar estimate:** at an assumed **US$2–$5 per GH200 GPU-hour**, those figures imply:
- **Production pretraining/extensions:** roughly **$4–$10 million**.
- **Whole-project allocation:** roughly **$18–$45 million**.

That hourly range is an illustrative assumption, **not a price reported by the authors or their actual bill**; it also does not account for staff and other project costs.

**Carbon footprint:** the paper says Alps uses **carbon-free hydropower**, but supplies no emissions factor or lifecycle carbon accounting. It therefore does **not establish a zero-tonne footprint**. [¶370] For sensitivity, every **1 g CO₂e/kWh** of assumed electricity carbon intensity would imply approximately **1.1 tonnes CO₂e** for production training, or **5 tonnes CO₂e** for the whole-project electricity estimate. Hardware manufacturing and other lifecycle emissions would be additional.

So the defensible summary is: **several million dollars for production training, potentially tens of millions for the full campaign under illustrative compute pricing; no substantiated tonnes-of-CO₂ total is available.**

runs.question: dpo-derivation
runs.text:
The sigmoid weight comes from differentiating \(-\log \sigma(z)\): its derivative is \(-\sigma(-z)\). Here, \(z\) is the preferred response’s implicit reward minus the dispreferred response’s implicit reward. Applying the chain rule gives exactly the Section 4 gradient. [¶33][¶37]

### 1. Define the margin for one preference pair

For a fixed example \((x,y_w,y_l)\), write Eq. (7) as
\[
\ell_\theta=-\log\sigma(z_\theta),
\]
where
\[
z_\theta
=
\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}
-
\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}.
\]
The full loss is \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[\ell_\theta]\). [¶33]

Using the paper’s implicit reward definition,
\[
\hat r_\theta(x,y)
=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)},
\]
we have \(z_\theta=\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)\). [¶38]

### 2. Differentiate the outer function

The sigmoid identities
\[
\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)),
\qquad
1-\sigma(z)=\sigma(-z)
\]
give
\[
\frac{d}{dz}[-\log\sigma(z)]
=
-\frac{\sigma'(z)}{\sigma(z)}
=
-(1-\sigma(z))
=
-\sigma(-z).
\]

Thus, by the chain rule,
\[
\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta
=
-\sigma(-z_\theta)\,\nabla_\theta z_\theta.
\]

### 3. Differentiate the margin

The reference policy is fixed, so its log-probabilities have zero gradient with respect to \(\theta\). Therefore,
\[
\nabla_\theta z_\theta
=
\beta\left[
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)
-
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)
\right].
\]

Substituting this and
\[
-z_\theta=\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)
\]
into the previous expression yields
\[
\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta
=
-\beta\,
\sigma\!\left(
\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)
\right)
\left[
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)
-
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)
\right].
\]

### 4. Average over the dataset

Because the offline dataset distribution does not depend on \(\theta\), take the expectation of the per-example gradient:
\[
\boxed{
\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DPO}}
=
-\beta\,\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}\!\left[
\sigma\!\left(
\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)
\right)
\left(
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)
-
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)
\right)
\right].
}
\]
This is the gradient displayed in Section 4. [¶37]

**Why the weight makes sense:** if the model incorrectly assigns the loser a higher implicit reward, the sigmoid weight is large; if the winner already has a much higher implicit reward, the weight approaches zero. Gradient descent therefore emphasizes incorrectly ordered pairs. [¶38]

**A sign-error warning:** Appendix A.4 contains sign inconsistencies: Eq. (21) reverses the margin relative to Eq. (7), and its later displayed sigmoid has the opposite sign from Section 4. The derivation above starts directly from Eq. (7) and recovers the Section 4 expression. [¶169][¶173][¶37]

For the **Reddit TL;DR summarization DPO run**, Appendix B gives:

| Optimizer | **RMSprop** |
